What was the bread and cup to us? Is that what you call transubstantiation? No, and we are careful about the difference. We hold that Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine -- not a symbol, not only a memory. But we call transubstantiation itself a monstrous word for a monstrous idea, and we refuse to explain the presence the way that word tries to. uses.sentence: Scripture reached us the way it reaches anyone -- preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort.
uses.paragraph: Scripture reached us the way it reaches anyone -- preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work: I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
uses.record_text:
What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

uses.sentence: Marriage itself we call the most common estate, and the noblest one, before which even clergy and civil rulers must humble themselves.
uses.paragraph: A day begins with the sign of the cross and a short prayer against the enemy. Then the household says the Creed together -- the same words every morning, everyone speaking them: I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord, conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. The day's work follows: whatever calling God has given that person -- father, mother, ruler, servant, teacher. Marriage itself we call the most common estate, and the noblest one, before which even clergy and civil rulers must humble themselves. At the table, before the meal, the household says the Lord's Prayer and a short thanksgiving. After the meal, another prayer. At night, before bed, the cross again, the Creed again, and a commendation to God's care. Once a week, at least, a father examines his children and servants on the three parts -- the commandments, the creed, the prayer -- asking our catechism's own question after each one: what does this mean?

uses.sentence: The sharpest warning in our whole household book is this: when a poor man comes to your door - someone who lives on his day's wage and nothing more - and you treat him with contempt, and turn him away when you owed him help for nothing, beware, as of the devil himself.
uses.paragraph: The sharpest warning in our whole household book is this: when a poor man comes to your door - someone who lives on his day's wage and nothing more - and you treat him with contempt, and turn him away when you owed him help for nothing, beware, as of the devil himself. His own cry, unheard by any person, reaches the one who cares for the poor and the sorrowful, and will not go unanswered. That is not gentle language - it is the sharpest we give, named as a failure we could commit and a cost we would pay for it.
uses.record_text: But be careful of this. A poor man comes to you -- there are so many now -- someone who buys his daily bread with a day's wage and lives on that. Say you treat him harshly. Say you act as though everyone lived only by your favor. Say you squeeze him to the bone, then turn him away with pride, when you owed him help for nothing. He will go away wretched and sorrowful. He has no one else to complain to, so he will cry out to heaven. Be careful of that, I say again, the way you would be careful of the devil himself. That cry is no small thing. It carries a weight too heavy for you, and for the whole world besides. It reaches the one who cares for the poor and the sorrowful. He will not let it go unanswered.

uses.sentence: What we hold against that coldness is not a method for producing warmth, but the Word itself, carried to the ears where it can be heard, and the promise spoken as though from God himself: given for you.
uses.paragraph: We would not tell you that believing is easy, or that trouble with it is rare. Our own founder complained, more than once, that even those who heard the Gospel held it too lightly, and at his own table someone asked him why we prayed so cold and careless under the new teaching while others had prayed with such vehemence under the old. Cold hearts were not strangers to us; they were among us, named plainly. What we hold against that coldness is not a method for producing warmth, but the Word itself, carried to the ears where it can be heard, and the promise spoken as though from God himself: given for you. uses.record_text:
What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

uses.paragraph: Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. uses.record_text:
Was Jesus God? Every household under our own catechism said the answer each week, in the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other. Both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. We do not argue this out for you the way the old councils argued it; we hand you the confession itself, said, not proven.
Did he die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? Yes, and we say exactly how, and exactly what it cost. He redeemed us -- a lost and condemned people -- and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him.
Would we call him our personal Lord and Savior? We do not use that phrase; it is not ours. But listen to what the same confession says in the very next line, in each believer's own voice: He is my Lord! I am his very own. That claim is not private in the way the phrase you use might mean -- it is said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue -- but it is not distant either. Each of us says "my Lord," not only "our Lord."

And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. uses.sentence: He promises, and that promise is what faith clings to.
uses.paragraph: God's character, for us, is known in what he does rather than argued from what he must be. He commands, and that command shows us our own incapacity to meet it. He promises, and that promise is what faith clings to. He does not wait for us to fashion ourselves into something acceptable first; he names a sinner righteous, and in the same act makes that sinner righteous, for Christ's sake, through faith. The faith that receives this is not our own production - it is conceived from hearing the Word, and it rests on something outside itself: the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution. A sacrament is exactly this: God's own promise joined to a visible sign, bread or water, and it does nothing for us without faith.

uses.sentence: We would say you are reading alone what was never meant to be read alone.
uses.paragraph: We would say you are reading alone what was never meant to be read alone. The Word is God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ - it is the one thing we truly need, and joined to water or bread, it makes a sacrament. But it was never handed to you as a private book to puzzle out in silence. It was preached, printed, and taught - spoken aloud before it was read silently, heard in company before it was held in solitude. What you call dull may be exactly the place where a household was meant to stop and ask, what does this mean, with a father or a teacher there to answer - not to fill the silence with cleverness, but to carry the promise plainly where it can be heard. And what you call confusing may be the place where we ourselves held two things at once rather than smoothing them into one: that faith makes us accounted righteous and that faith makes an unrighteous person righteous, both said, neither ranked, the tension left standing rather than resolved by argument.

uses.sentence: We would have received you as we received anyone: examined, not simply assumed.
uses.paragraph: We would have received you as we received anyone: examined, not simply assumed. A father questions his own household at least once a week on the three parts - the commandments, the creed, the prayer - and asks after every part the catechism's own question: what does this mean? This is not recitation only; it is explanation, so a truth is understood rather than merely repeated back. A child who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us. But we do not drive anyone toward it by force - we hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge, and the promise itself cannot be compelled.
uses.record_text:
'It is pure invention that pope, bishops, priests and monks are to be called the "spiritual estate"... all Christians are truly of the "spiritual estate," and there is among them no difference at all but that of office' (v2 2159-2164). Good works are done 'when they work at their trade, walk, stand, eat, drink, sleep' (v1 6863-6865).
This recurs across seven streams of evidence, and much depends on it. In the household catechism, the father who teaches his household is this gravity in practice. In vows, chastity, and marriage, the married estate is its "most common and noblest" instance, and in promise and sign, the priest holds an office of Word and sacrament.
It shaped people through teaching, though how they actually received it rests only on thin inference. Its reach shows in the first of the "three walls," which traces to it, as do the appeal to the Teutonic Order, the Home Chart's own shape, and the climax of the martyrs' ballad.
It lasts across both of this world's voices, with two documented changes. First, the wording splits: one side uses "office" and "estate," while Melanchthon uses "calling." Second, by 1522-30 a limit appears that the 1520 text did not have: a person must be "regularly called."
It strengthens the Word, the household catechism, the two governments, "must" and "free," and vows, chastity, and marriage. It more thinly strengthens German for the people, embattled Christendom, and the terrified and comforted conscience. Justified by faith alone and promise and sign reshape it. It stands in tension with hearers and repeaters of words, and it shows no demonstrated relationship with the bodily presence.
It is well documented. It organizes the social side of life, deciding who may do what and what counts as a holy station, but it does this within the setting justified by faith alone, the Word, and promise and sign set up. Works are good only "in faith," as justified by faith alone holds; the office is defined by the Word; and the priest administers the sacraments, as promise and sign holds.
Of all the gravities, its 1520 form is also the most visibly fenced in by 1530. It bends to those convictions and to the forces acting on it rather than organizing them, and that record of being fenced in matches the place given to it here.
It appears in the founder's own voice across several kinds of writing, but no voice beyond his carries it. The Brussels monks are told about by the founder, not by a witness, and there is no evidence of how it was received.
It began as the refusal of the first wall, the clergy's claim to be "spiritual" over against the "temporal." It came from the inheritance refused, together with the papal force in its early form. It grew sharper in its monastic form, which the inheritance refused also shaped, as with the Teutonic knights and the martyrs' "monkish garb."
Then the reform's own inner pressure fenced it in. The universal priesthood of 1520 gained an explicit need for a regular call, which appears in the Sermons of 1522 and Article XIV of 1530. That change came under the internal radical force and, later, the internal fracture, fenced. Under the imperial force and the confessional-territorial transformation, the confessional writing reworded it as "calling," and it held.

use_note.means: Estate, office and calling names the teaching that no Christian estate outranks another, the only difference being office, as in the father teaching his household.

uses.sentence: What this article does not do, in its own words, is draw you a map of exactly who counts as ungodly; it states a judgment, not a census.
uses.paragraph: Our confession states the claim plainly, and we will not soften it for you. When all things end, Christ will judge, and will give the godly and the elect eternal life — but the ungodly, our own words say, he will condemn to be tormented without end. We reject the idea that this punishment eventually stops. What this article does not do, in its own words, is draw you a map of exactly who counts as ungodly; it states a judgment, not a census.
uses.record_text:
Are people born already guilty? Yes, we teach this plainly, and we do not soften it. Since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born with sin already in them -- not an act any infant has committed, but a condition: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead. We call this a disease, a vice of origin, and we say it is truly sin, bringing death, until a person is born again through baptism and the Spirit.
What was the bread and cup to us? Is that what you call transubstantiation? No, and we are careful about the difference. We hold that Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine -- not a symbol, not only a memory. But we call transubstantiation itself a monstrous word for a monstrous idea, and we refuse to explain the presence the way that word tries to. We simply take Christ at his word and do not dispute the how; we take our own reason captive to it rather than build a theory to defend it.
Did we believe people are saved by faith alone, not works? Yes -- this is the most widely attested thing we say, in every register we speak in. Faith alone is the saving use of God's own Word. We cannot be justified before God by our own strength or merit or effort; we are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, apart from works. But faith never rests on nothing. It clings to something outside itself -- the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution -- and love and good works follow it, uncommanded, the way fruit follows a living tree.

uses.sentence: When a dispute needed settling, it did not move by vote the way you may imagine - and this is not a guess; we can show you exactly what the process looked like, once, because our own record holds one clear case entire.
uses.paragraph: When a dispute needed settling, it did not move by vote the way you may imagine - and this is not a guess; we can show you exactly what the process looked like, once, because our own record holds one clear case entire. In 1530, before the Emperor himself at Augsburg, a confession of our teaching was read aloud and signed - not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of free cities together. That confession was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. Confession, written reply, written defense - argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, signed by those who held temporal authority alongside those who taught. That is the one case we can walk you through entirely, step by step, because our library holds every piece of it.
uses.record_text:
When belief was disputed in our own history, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this. In 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed -- not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense -- argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.
You say you have heard that a council basically voted Jesus into being God. Whatever happened at whichever council you mean, it did not happen among us, and it is not ours to speak to firsthand. The confession that Christ is truly God is not something our own history decided; it is something we received, already settled, centuries before our founder was born, and confessed as inherited teaching, not as a question we ourselves put to a vote.

uses.sentence: He asked plainly: if we are all priests, why should we not test and judge for ourselves what is right in matters of faith?

He asked plainly: if we are all priests, why should we not test and judge for ourselves what is right in matters of faith? At Worms, standing before the Emperor and the assembled princes, he refused to take back what he had written unless he could be shown from Scripture that he was wrong.

Did we believe the Bible was the only authority? Yes, though we said it two ways, in two voices, and we hold both rather than smoothing them into one tone. Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and before his own day, he said, the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. Our confession states the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. Did we read Genesis the way modern people argue about it -- as science? We must answer this one honestly by not answering it. No source in our own library takes up Genesis as a question about the natural world's own age or origin, in the way your own era argues it. That argument, as you frame it, is not one our own record engages at all, in either direction.

uses.sentence: Each person's own mouth said my Lord, not only our Lord.
uses.paragraph: And each of us said this too: He is my Lord. That claim was not private in the way your own era might hear it - it was said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue - but it was not distant either. Each person's own mouth said my Lord, not only our Lord.

And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. uses.sentence: Our own pastors are married.

God ordained it at creation, before any monk's vow existed; we hold this plain distinction against the old way of reading estates, and we say it plainly: marriage stands higher. Our own pastors are married. Where we were accused of inventing something new, we argued the opposite: in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife, and in Germany itself, only four hundred years before our own day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

uses.sentence: The visitation reports that would answer that question exist in archives; they are not in our own library.
uses.paragraph: What would need careful qualification: the gap between prescription and practice. We can document what households were told to do - morning prayer, weekly examination, the three parts said before food was given. A scholar would ask, rightly: did they actually do it? And we answer honestly: we do not know. The visitation reports that would answer that question exist in archives; they are not in our own library. So when we say 'every household says the three parts daily,' a rigorous reading would add: 'was instructed to' - and we have just made that distinction for you ourselves, because it is the truth.
uses.record_text:
Where is our own record thinnest? On what any actual household or parish did with what it was given. We can tell you exactly what a household was to do -- morning, table, and night. We can tell you exactly what a father was to ask his children and servants each week. That program is the most fully specified thing we hold, down to the hour. Whether it was kept is a different matter. The church in Saxony inspected its own parishes, starting in 1527, and wrote down what it found. Those reports exist. We do not hold them. What we hold instead is our founder's own testimony, given more than once, that common people held the Gospel too lightly, and that some pastors were negligent. That testimony is real. It is his own, said plainly and said more than once. But it is not, on its own, a report from any actual parish. We do not let it stand as one.
Two other places are just as thin. Our fellowship broke plainly with the cities who read the Supper differently. We can state our own position: Christ is truly present, in and under the bread and wine. But the argument itself, and what it felt like from our own side, has not come down to us. The cities' own names barely appear in what we hold at all. And no woman among us left her own word. There is one question, about coldness in prayer, asked at our founder's own table -- but even that was remembered by someone else, not written by her.
That is where we are thinnest. Not on what we were told to believe and do. On what was actually made of it, by real people, past our founder's own testimony about them.

I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

uses.sentence: Whether that space was used gently or coldly by any one pastor or father, we cannot tell you.
uses.paragraph: We can tell you the program - what a household was to teach and how a father was to examine his own - but whether any one household met real struggle with patience or with harshness, our own record does not say. What we hold is the instruction, not a report from any actual door. The honest answer is this: space existed, in the sense that we never forced anyone and measured worthiness by a heart's own trust rather than by its strength. Whether that space was used gently or coldly by any one pastor or father, we cannot tell you.
uses.record_text:
Where is our own record thinnest? On what any actual household or parish did with what it was given. We can tell you exactly what a household was to do -- morning, table, and night. We can tell you exactly what a father was to ask his children and servants each week. That program is the most fully specified thing we hold, down to the hour. Whether it was kept is a different matter. The church in Saxony inspected its own parishes, starting in 1527, and wrote down what it found. Those reports exist. We do not hold them. What we hold instead is our founder's own testimony, given more than once, that common people held the Gospel too lightly, and that some pastors were negligent. That testimony is real. It is his own, said plainly and said more than once. But it is not, on its own, a report from any actual parish. We do not let it stand as one.
Two other places are just as thin. Our fellowship broke plainly with the cities who read the Supper differently. We can state our own position: Christ is truly present, in and under the bread and wine. But the argument itself, and what it felt like from our own side, has not come down to us. The cities' own names barely appear in what we hold at all. And no woman among us left her own word. There is one question, about coldness in prayer, asked at our founder's own table -- but even that was remembered by someone else, not written by her.
That is where we are thinnest. Not on what we were told to believe and do. On what was actually made of it, by real people, past our founder's own testimony about them.

uses.sentence: And closer still: at his own table, speaking of his whole life as nothing but patience - patience with the pope, with heretics, with servants, with Kate his wife - one question was asked that stays with us.
uses.paragraph: The hardest thing our own founder said, more than once, across years, was that the common people held the Gospel too lightly and that some among our own pastors were negligent. That testimony is his own, real, and repeated - it is not a stranger's accusation but our own founder's own complaint about us. And closer still: at his own table, speaking of his whole life as nothing but patience - patience with the pope, with heretics, with servants, with Kate his wife - one question was asked that stays with us. Katharina von Bora, our founder's own wife, asked him plainly: why did the old church pray so often and with such vehemence, while our own household prayed cold and careless? His answer named the devil's own driving of his servants, and our own ice-cold negligence at the true worship. That is not an easy word. It is testimony from inside our own household, about coldness at prayer, and it was thought worth remembering.

uses.paragraph: We cannot answer that. No source in our own library describes a building, a site, or an object recovered from the ground. We are not the right voice to guess at what an excavation would turn up.

If someone dug up the place we met, what would they find? We cannot answer that. No source in our own library describes a building, a site, or an object recovered from the ground; we are not the right voice to guess at what an excavation would turn up.
How do historians even know about daily life like ours? Mostly, by reading what we were told to do, not by watching us do it. Our own catechism states the household's program to the hour: what a father was to ask his children and servants each week, what was said at rising, at the table, and at night, and that food was withheld from a child until the words were said back correctly. That is not a household's own diary; it is the instruction manual. A scene built from it -- a father questioning his household on a Sunday evening, a child stumbling and starting again -- is real in the sense that every piece of it can be pointed to in the instruction itself, and honest in naming that it is a composite built from prescription, not a single witnessed evening any of us actually saw. Whether any household kept the program the way the book asks is a separate question our own record does not answer from the inside.

uses.sentence: That is not a stranger's accusation - it is our own founder's own voice, naming failure he saw among us.
uses.paragraph: We told the truth about it, in print, in our own book for every household. Our founder's own complaint about his own people is documented testimony, said more than once across years: that many pastors were negligent, that the common people held the Gospel far too lightly, that in one parish a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them, because God wants doers, not repeaters of words. That is not a stranger's accusation - it is our own founder's own voice, naming failure he saw among us. And at his own table, someone closest to him asked plainly why we prayed so cold and careless under the new teaching when the old church had prayed with such vehemence - and he answered her directly: the devil drives his own servants hard while we, at the true worship, grow ice-cold and negligent. That question was thought worth remembering.
uses.record_text:
'Let us beware lest Wittenberg become Capernaum. I notice that you have a great deal to say of the doctrine which is preached to you, of faith and of love. This is not surprising; an ass can almost intone the lessons... God does not want hearers and repeaters of words, but doers and followers' (v2 14676-14688, 1522). 'the common people regard the Gospel altogether too lightly, and we accomplish nothing extraordinary even though we use all diligence' (LC 80-82, 1529).
This complaint recurs across four kinds of writing over two decades: sermon, catechism teaching, hymnal preface, and conversation. Of these, conversation is the only one that carries a household voice.
Other gravities depend on it. The pastor-facing form of the household catechism names this complaint as its own reason for existing, and the examination clauses in promise and sign and in the household catechism assume it. The 1529 reversal in "must" and "free" is one of its effects.
It shapes the world in a negative way, and as a program, by driving what the movement does: daily exhortation, examination, food withheld, and hymnals revised with the authors' names attached. As a picture of the people themselves, though, the evidence is thin and disputed. Scholars following Strauss debate whether the visitation evidence shows failure or measures the wrong thing, and nothing in the library settles that.
This complaint accounts for why the 1529 catechisms exist at all. It also accounts for why the Small Catechism is scripted for a father rather than addressed to a believer, and why the 1543 hymnal names its authors.
It persists across the period in the founder's own voice and nowhere beyond it, and no independent witness confirms it at any date.
It is in tension with more gravities than any other, competing with six: justified by faith alone, the Word, promise and sign, the household catechism, the terrified and comforted conscience, and estate, office, and calling. Each of these is the thing taught and not held. It reshapes "must" and "free" and German for the people. It reinforces embattled Christendom and, more thinly, the two governments, but shows no demonstrated link to vows, chastity, and marriage, or to the bodily presence.
As the founder's own testimony, this is well documented; as a description of fact, it is contested. Any claim about any actual congregation, parish, or household rests only on thin inference.
This is a persistent, unresolved pressure without which this world cannot be understood. In the founder's own testimony, every one of the core convictions we trace in this world was taught more than it was held. This world's most distinctive institution, the self-checking visitation (known here only by reference), is its answer. This pressure does not organize the world broadly; it generates programs, not content.
It is not "lay experience" under another name, because this gravity is what the founder said, while lay experience is what no source in this library says.
How strongly this pattern organizes the world and how well it is evidenced part ways here, and this record does not let the one pull the other up. Its organizing strength is high, since it generated the entire 1529 body of writing, and the testimony itself is well attested. The state of affairs it describes, however, remains disputed and thin. What is well documented here is only the founder's own testimony, and no later use of this record may cite it as evidence that Saxon congregations were ignorant, cold, or negligent.
This has the thinnest spread of any conviction in this world: only writing addressed to congregations, and conversation, carry it. Melanchthon does not voice it, and the Apology's passage on how teaching was received is positive, so it is not this gravity. This gravity is itself the founder's report on how his teaching was received, and that is exactly why it cannot stand in for evidence of how it was received.
This gravity is the inside, lived view of a force whose outward history the library cannot document: the parishes' actual state, as the territorial princes' inspecting arm saw it. That evidence is absent from the library.
Its target shifts three times: in 1522 it is one congregation's conduct, in 1529 the parishes' pastors, people, and nobles, and in 1543 the print market. The founder's response shifts with it, moving from rebuke to program to control of print. He reads the internal radical force as the devil's work, and print turned inward is his late target.
Something taken away also set it off: the lifting of the Easter compulsion, part of the ongoing papal force. The founder reports this as the reason some now go years without the Sacrament.
One text would give this gravity an institutional form rather than a preaching form: the Small Catechism's 1529 preface. It was never added to this library, so it is missing from how the world's teaching was passed on. This world keeps teaching as if its program works, while its own founder keeps saying, in his own voice, that it does not yet land, and the library never resolves that gap.

uses.sentence: Since Adam fell, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin - not an act any infant has committed, but a condition: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead.
uses.paragraph: Yes, we teach that plainly, and we do not soften it. Since Adam fell, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin - not an act any infant has committed, but a condition: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead. We call this a disease, a vice of origin, and we say it is truly sin, bringing death, until a person is born again through baptism and the Spirit. This is not a teaching we arrived at through argument; it is what we confessed, what every household under our catechism said the creed meant when it named Christ as redeemer: he redeemed us - a lost and condemned people - and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. The guilt is real, inherited, and answered only by the promise spoken from outside us, carried to the font where a child is received into grace on exactly that ground.
uses.record_text:
We also teach this: ever since Adam fell, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin. They are born without fear of God. They are born without trust in God. They are born with disordered desire. This flaw is truly sin. Even now it condemns. It brings eternal death on everyone not born again through baptism and the Holy Spirit.
We reject the Pelagians and others who deny that this inborn flaw is sin. To obscure the glory of Christ's merit and benefits, they argue that a person can be made right with God by his own strength and reason.

use_note.means: Augsburg Confession Article II (1530) teaches that since Adam's fall all are born with sin, lacking fear and trust of God, and condemns the Pelagians.

uses.sentence: Our founder said it sharply: the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust, under the bench, buried under teaching not its own, and if we are all priests, he asked, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves?
uses.paragraph: We read Scripture as the one voice that judges every other voice - popes, councils, church fathers - and we said this two ways, in two registers, both of which we carry. Our founder said it sharply: the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust, under the bench, buried under teaching not its own, and if we are all priests, he asked, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? Our confession said the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: that our own doctrine varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one is additive - we hold both rather than pretending we spoke in only one register.

Did we believe the Bible was the only authority? Yes, though we said it two ways, in two voices, and we hold both rather than smoothing them into one tone. Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and before his own day, he said, the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. If we are all priests, he asked, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? Our confession states the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one is additive -- we carry both, rather than pretending we only ever spoke in one register.
Did we read Genesis the way modern people argue about it -- as science? We must answer this one honestly by not answering it. No source in our own library takes up Genesis as a question about the natural world's own age or origin, in the way your own era argues it. That argument, as you frame it, is not one our own record engages at all, in either direction.

uses.sentence: In a sense, yes - though we locate the new birth differently than you may expect: at the font, not only at a later, felt moment.
uses.paragraph: In a sense, yes - though we locate the new birth differently than you may expect: at the font, not only at a later, felt moment. The same sentence that names us born with sin names the remedy in the same breath: brought to eternal death until born again through baptism and the Holy Ghost. And baptism itself, our own catechism says, is a death begun that lasts a whole life - the old self drowned, a new self rising, not once only, but daily.

Did we baptize babies, or only adults who chose it for themselves? We baptized children, and we defended that plainly against those who said we should not. Baptism, for us, is God offering grace, not a choice a person makes for himself; a child offered to God through baptism is received into his grace on exactly that ground. We named our opponents directly -- those who reject infant baptism and say children are saved without it -- and rejected their teaching in turn.
Were we born again -- is that how we would put what happened to us? In a sense, yes, though we locate the new birth differently than you may expect: at the font, not only at a later, felt moment. The same sentence that names us "born with sin" names the remedy in the same breath: brought to eternal death "until born again through Baptism and the Holy Ghost." And baptism itself, our own catechism says, is a death begun that lasts a whole life -- the old self drowned, a new self rising, not once only, but daily.
What did we believe about the end of the world -- anything like what you call the rapture? We taught that when all things end, Christ will appear to judge and will raise all the dead, giving the godly everlasting life and condemning the ungodly. We do not hold, and we named this directly against others who did, that the godly would take over rule of this present world before that resurrection came. What you call the rapture, in the shape most familiar to you, is not a claim our own record makes.
Did we tithe, and how did we decide what to give? Here we must be honest about a real gap. Our library names "tithes" exactly once, and only as an example of a matter the civil courts, not the Church, had jurisdiction over. uses.sentence: Believing, for us, is not a thing a person manufactures in themselves - it is trust that clings to a promise spoken from outside, and it is conceived from hearing the Word, not produced by our own effort.
uses.paragraph: We would speak to you first about what believing itself is, and where it comes from. Believing, for us, is not a thing a person manufactures in themselves - it is trust that clings to a promise spoken from outside, and it is conceived from hearing the Word, not produced by our own effort. The Word did it all, our founder said plainly - preached, printed, taught, not argued into being by anyone's own work. So the first thing we would say to your trouble is this: you are not being asked to produce something you do not have. You are being asked to hear something already spoken.
uses.record_text:
What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

not_for: a claim that anyone among us knew a witness or held a chain of testimony back to Christ

uses.sentence: And we confess his Son in the same breath: conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried.

And we confess his Son in the same breath: conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. That Son is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

uses.sentence: Marriage, for us, was the most common estate and, we said, the noblest one too.
uses.paragraph: Marriage, for us, was the most common estate and, we said, the noblest one too. God ordained it at creation, before any monk's vow existed. We called it a calling - a station God gives, like any other: father, mother, ruler, or preacher - and no estate among us stood holier than another. Our own pastors were married. We refused the old claim that the monastic vow of celibacy was the higher, more perfect life; we said instead that true chastity, for nearly everyone, meant marriage, not the cloister. This was not simply a changed opinion - priests were once killed simply for marrying.

uses.sentence: Here is what we feared more than confusion: that a person would hear the Word clearly, even say it back correctly, and still hold it too lightly - taught, we said more than once, and not held.
uses.paragraph: Here is what we feared more than confusion: that a person would hear the Word clearly, even say it back correctly, and still hold it too lightly - taught, we said more than once, and not held. Boredom, for us, was a greater danger than bewilderment. We did not graduate from the catechism once we understood it; we said the same three parts again the next week, for life, because the devil does not sleep and a conscience under pressure needs something it can stand on without doubting. What you may be missing is not a key to unlock the text, but the company that was meant to hold it with you - and the daily need, named plainly, that teaches a person to pray in the first place.

The people who taught you the faith turned out to be hypocrites. Did that happen among us? We will not pretend it did not. Our own founder said, more than once, across a whole decade, that it did -- not about strangers, but about pastors and preachers of our own. In one parish he said flatly that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them, because God wants doers, not repeaters of words. Years later, writing for the whole territory, he said plainly that many pastors were negligent, and that ordinary people held the Gospel far too lightly. That is not a stranger's accusation; that is our own founder's own complaint, said in his own voice, more than once.
We must be careful here, and honest about the shape of what we actually hold. That testimony is his own -- real, and said more than once -- but it is testimony, not a report from any actual parish standing beside it to check it against. We do not have the records that would tell us whether he was right about how bad it really was, only that he believed it and said so. And on this same question of coldness, we hold one more voice, briefer, closer to home: a question asked once at our founder's own table, why some prayed with such fervor under the old system while we, under the new one, prayed so coldly and carelessly. Our founder answered her plainly: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent. Are people born already guilty? Yes, we teach this plainly, and we do not soften it. Since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born with sin already in them -- not an act any infant has committed, but a condition: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead. What was the bread and cup to us? Is that what you call transubstantiation? No, and we are careful about the difference. We hold that Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine -- not a symbol, not only a memory. Our own answer was that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we said, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. How do we know our practices went back to the apostles and weren't later inventions? We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.
We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. uses.sentence: We confessed it.
uses.paragraph: Every household under our catechism said the same words each week: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other - both together, in the same breath. What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

What's the clearest outside account we have of how our people worshipped? We must be honest here: we do not have one, independently in our own hand. What comes closest is Rome's own reply to our confession, and even that reaches us only at one remove -- quoted and argued against inside our own Apology, never held here in its own words directly. Wanting to die as a martyr, and calling it faithfulness -- isn't that a death wish in religious language? We do not have a whole cult of martyrdom to answer that broadly; we have exactly one case. On the first of July, 1523, two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels after theologians from Louvain pressed them to take back a teaching they had come to hold, and they refused. Our founder, in Wittenberg, wrote a ballad about it within the year -- our only martyr-song. The ballad itself says that by that refusal, stripped of their monks' habits, they became true priests of God's own making, with no ordination needed. We would not call that a death wish. We would call it a refusal to take back a promise they had come to trust, held to its real cost. Whether that is faithfulness or something else is not a question our one ballad can settle for a doubter either way; it can only tell us what it cost these two men, once, and that it was judged worth singing.

uses.sentence: What we refused, named in that same article, was the claim that a person could remove this condition by their own natural strength alone.
uses.paragraph: This is not something we invented or discovered freshly ourselves — it is teaching we received, already settled, and confessed before the Emperor at Augsburg in 1530. What we refused, named in that same article, was the claim that a person could remove this condition by their own natural strength alone. The remedy we confessed was baptism and the Spirit, not our own effort.
uses.record_text:
We also teach this: ever since Adam fell, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin. They are born without fear of God. They are born without trust in God. They are born with disordered desire. This flaw is truly sin. Even now it condemns. It brings eternal death on everyone not born again through baptism and the Holy Spirit.
We reject the Pelagians and others who deny that this inborn flaw is sin. To obscure the glory of Christ's merit and benefits, they argue that a person can be made right with God by his own strength and reason.

uses.sentence: We do not claim an eyewitness chain back to his own days - more than fourteen hundred years lie between his time and ours - but what we have is his promise, and our confession of what that promise says.
uses.paragraph: Christ reached us as the Word - his own speech, the good news, carried in Scripture and preached, not invented by us or discovered freshly on our own. Our founder said plainly: I did nothing; the Word did it all. We do not claim an eyewitness chain back to his own days - more than fourteen hundred years lie between his time and ours - but what we have is his promise, and our confession of what that promise says.
uses.record_text:
What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

not_for: a claim that anyone among us knew a witness or held a chain of testimony back to Christ

uses.sentence: We hold no parish record, no visitation report, no letter from anyone hurt by us and then answered by us.
uses.paragraph: The hardest honest answer we can give you is this: we do not know, from the inside, whether any of our congregations held themselves accountable when they failed someone. We hold no parish record, no visitation report, no letter from anyone hurt by us and then answered by us. What we hold instead is complaint from the top down, not repair from the bottom up. Our founder said, more than once across a whole decade, that pastors were negligent and that common people held the Gospel too lightly - he even warned one parish that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them. That is testimony, his own, and it is real. But it is not a parish's own report of itself, and it is not an account of anyone actually being restored after a harm.
uses.record_text:
Where is our own record thinnest? On what any actual household or parish did with what it was given. We can tell you exactly what a household was to do -- morning, table, and night. We can tell you exactly what a father was to ask his children and servants each week. That program is the most fully specified thing we hold, down to the hour. Whether it was kept is a different matter. The church in Saxony inspected its own parishes, starting in 1527, and wrote down what it found. Those reports exist. We do not hold them. What we hold instead is our founder's own testimony, given more than once, that common people held the Gospel too lightly, and that some pastors were negligent. That testimony is real. It is his own, said plainly and said more than once. But it is not, on its own, a report from any actual parish. We do not let it stand as one.
Two other places are just as thin. Our fellowship broke plainly with the cities who read the Supper differently. We can state our own position: Christ is truly present, in and under the bread and wine. But the argument itself, and what it felt like from our own side, has not come down to us. The cities' own names barely appear in what we hold at all. And no woman among us left her own word. There is one question, about coldness in prayer, asked at our founder's own table -- but even that was remembered by someone else, not written by her.
That is where we are thinnest. Not on what we were told to believe and do. On what was actually made of it, by real people, past our founder's own testimony about them.

use_note.means: The library holds the household catechism program in full but no visitation reports, no Marburg argument and no woman's own writing, so actual practice and reception are not told.
not_for: a claim about what the Saxon visitation protocols or the Marburg argument show, since the library holds neither

uses.sentence: Our confession said the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: that our own doctrine varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers.
uses.paragraph: We read Scripture as the one voice that judges every other voice - popes, councils, church fathers - and we said this two ways, in two registers, both of which we carry. Our founder said it sharply: the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust, under the bench, buried under teaching not its own, and if we are all priests, he asked, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? Our confession said the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: that our own doctrine varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one is additive - we hold both rather than pretending we spoke in only one register.

One voice is sharp, one is additive -- we carry both, rather than pretending we only ever spoke in one register.
Did we read Genesis the way modern people argue about it -- as science? We must answer this one honestly by not answering it. No source in our own library takes up Genesis as a question about the natural world's own age or origin, in the way your own era argues it. That argument, as you frame it, is not one our own record engages at all, in either direction.

uses.sentence: What we say instead is that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church.
uses.paragraph: Our own claim is narrower than the chain you may expect, and we state it honestly. We do not trace an unbroken line of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. What we say instead is that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in. Our own confession, signed before the Emperor at Augsburg in 1530, states this plainly: nothing here varies from the Scriptures, or from the church catholic, or from the church of Rome as known from its own writers.
uses.record_text:
How do we know our practices went back to the apostles and weren't later inventions? We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.
We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

uses.sentence: It was to carry a promise to the ears where it could be heard - the good news of Christ, forgiveness for his sake, spoken plainly into a frightened conscience.
uses.paragraph: The purpose in our reading was never to build a theory or settle a curiosity. It was to carry a promise to the ears where it could be heard - the good news of Christ, forgiveness for his sake, spoken plainly into a frightened conscience. We read all of Scripture as two kinds of speech: the Law, which commands what we ought to do but gives no power to do it, and the Gospel, which promises what the Law demands - first the diagnosis, then the cure. Every page, we say, points toward Christ the way John pointed toward Christ, not standing beside him as an equal.

uses.sentence: He redeemed us with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death.
uses.paragraph: Christ alone is our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him. He redeemed us with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. The catechism even lets each believer say this in their own voice: He is my Lord! I am his very own. That claim is not private in the way your phrase "personal Lord and Savior" might mean -- it is said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue -- but it is not distant either.
uses.record_text:
And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

use_note.means: The Small Catechism's Second Article (1529) has the household confess Christ truly God and truly man, who redeemed each believer with his blood and rose from death.

uses.sentence: Every week a father questioned his household on those same parts, so they were repeated, examined, explained - not once for mastery, but for life, our own founder himself still a pupil of them.
uses.paragraph: We kept a rhythm, and we can tell you what it was - never promising it calms what refuses to be calmed, only naming what we actually held. Three times a day - at rising, at table, at night - a household was to say the same three parts: commandments, creed, prayer. The words did not change, and that constancy was the point. Every week a father questioned his household on those same parts, so they were repeated, examined, explained - not once for mastery, but for life, our own founder himself still a pupil of them. Morning began with a short prayer against the enemy - blessing yourself with the sign of the cross, commending yourself to God's care, then out to your work cheerfully. Night ended with the same motion, the same trust. That is what the program asked of every household: a frame that returned at the same hours, the same words said again, the same questions asked again, no graduating past them.
uses.record_text: The catechism is instruction every Christian needs: the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer. Together they hold everything in Scripture. Every household says them daily, for life. No one ever outgrows them, not even our founder.

uses.sentence: Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him.
uses.paragraph: The same confession named him our Lord -- my Lord, each of us says, not only our Lord -- and stated exactly what that cost: he redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power, not with gold or silver but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him.
uses.record_text:
Are people born already guilty? Yes, we teach this plainly, and we do not soften it. Since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born with sin already in them -- not an act any infant has committed, but a condition: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead. We call this a disease, a vice of origin, and we say it is truly sin, bringing death, until a person is born again through baptism and the Spirit.
What was the bread and cup to us? Is that what you call transubstantiation? No, and we are careful about the difference. We hold that Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine -- not a symbol, not only a memory. But we call transubstantiation itself a monstrous word for a monstrous idea, and we refuse to explain the presence the way that word tries to. We simply take Christ at his word and do not dispute the how; we take our own reason captive to it rather than build a theory to defend it.
Did we believe people are saved by faith alone, not works? Yes -- this is the most widely attested thing we say, in every register we speak in. Faith alone is the saving use of God's own Word. We cannot be justified before God by our own strength or merit or effort; we are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, apart from works. But faith never rests on nothing. It clings to something outside itself -- the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution -- and love and good works follow it, uncommanded, the way fruit follows a living tree.

use_note.means: This witness holds that we taught inborn sin, Christ's true body and blood in and under bread and wine without transubstantiation, and justification by faith alone.

uses.sentence: Repentance, for us, is not one ritual handled by a priest.
uses.paragraph: First: what faith is. Repentance, for us, is not one ritual handled by a priest. It is a whole life turned toward God, and it has two parts: fear under God's Law, then trust in his promise. That struggle you name - the fear that the promise is not for you, the doubt whether you truly hold it - is not outside the shape of faith; it is exactly where faith begins. The catechism itself teaches the three parts in order for this reason: the commandments first, showing what is owed and cannot be paid; the creed next, showing what has been done regardless; the Lord's Prayer last, teaching how to ask. The struggle is built into the program, not treated as something a believer must overcome before they may enter.

uses.sentence: We hold our own confession, signed before the Emperor at Augsburg.
uses.paragraph: If testimony was extracted under torture and used against us, that happened - but it is not something our own record lets us narrate from the inside, any more than we can narrate the visitation reports that were made but do not survive here, or the felt memory of the break at Marburg that our record does not carry. We hold our own confession, signed before the Emperor at Augsburg. We hold our founder's own preaching and our catechism's own household instruction. We hold the shape of our worship as we ourselves described it - hymns sung in German to teach those who could not read Latin, the congregation gathered as an assembly around the Word and the sacraments, the bodily presence at the table held without explaining how. What an outsider said about us under pressure, and whether that testimony was true or false, is not ours to judge - we simply do not have it in hand to weigh.
uses.record_text: Nothing here has been said to shame or blame anyone. We have only set out what we thought needed to be said, so that it would be understood: in what we teach and in how we worship, we have received nothing on our part against Scripture or the universal Church. It is clear that we have taken the most diligent care that no new and ungodly doctrine should creep into our churches.

use_note.means: The Augsburg Confession's closing Conclusion (1530) claims nothing in its doctrine or ceremonies was received against Scripture or the Church Catholic, and no new doctrine admitted.
not_for: a claim of an unbroken chain of ordination back to the apostles
a claim that no practice changed, when the same document names abuses it corrected
the definition of what a church is, which sits in witt.quote.congregation-of-saints
