uses.sentence: What we have is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
uses.paragraph: What did we have of Jesus ourselves? The Word - his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not discover it freshly on our own, and we do not pretend any of us knew someone who saw him; more than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says. Each week, every household under our catechism said the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary - conceived by the Holy Spirit, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried, and on the third day rose again from the dead. That confession is what we have. We do not argue the resurrection the way a historian weighs evidence; we confess it.
uses.record_text:
What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

use_note.means: This witness holds that Christ reached us through the preached and printed Word, that no eyewitness chain stands behind us, and that we confessed the resurrection rather than argued it.
not_for: a claim that anyone among us knew a witness or held a chain of testimony back to Christ
an argued historical case for the resurrection addressed to a doubter
the teaching on who Christ is and what he did, which sits in witt.dw.truly-god-and-truly-man

uses.sentence: I am his very own.
uses.paragraph: Every household under our catechism said the same words each week, in one voice: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other -- both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver; it cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him. And each of us says, in that same creed: He is my Lord! I am his very own. That claim is not private in the way you might think it -- it is said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue -- but it is not distant either; each believer says "my Lord," not only "our Lord."
uses.record_text:
And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

use_note.means: The Small Catechism's Second Article (1529) has the household confess Christ truly God and truly man, who redeemed each believer with his blood and rose from death.
not_for: a remembered personal saying of any individual, when this is recited household text
'He is my Lord' as the modern phrase 'personal Lord and Savior'
an argued or eyewitness case for the resurrection, when this is confession only
an argued defense of the Trinity as a formula, which no record holds and witt.dw.truly-god-and-truly-man names as absent

uses.sentence: In March of 1522, returning unbidden from the Wartburg to a Wittenberg turned disorderly under a colleague's own zealous leadership, our founder preached eight days running and told his own congregation to their faces that they had learned the words of the reform and not yet its love.
uses.paragraph: A pastor, once called, is owed honor and a decent living by the congregation. But our own founder did not spare him — when pastors were negligent, through pride of learning or through sheer sloth, he said so plainly, more than once, across years. In March of 1522, returning unbidden from the Wartburg to a Wittenberg turned disorderly under a colleague's own zealous leadership, our founder preached eight days running and told his own congregation to their faces that they had learned the words of the reform and not yet its love. That is not gentle language. That is a rebuke, spoken from the pulpit, to the people who had received him.
uses.record_text: Luther leaves the safety of the Wartburg without his prince's leave, rides back into a Wittenberg turned disorderly under a colleague's own zealous leadership, and preaches eight days running, telling his own congregation to their faces that they have learned the words of the reform and not yet its love.

use_note.means: In March 1522 Luther returned unbidden from the Wartburg and preached eight days in disordered Wittenberg, saying they had reform's words but not its love.

uses.sentence: Before the Emperor himself, at Augsburg in 1530, our confession was read aloud and signed -- not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of free cities, naming themselves together.
uses.paragraph: Before the Emperor himself, at Augsburg in 1530, our confession was read aloud and signed -- not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of free cities, naming themselves together. Its own conclusion states this: nothing here has been said to shame or blame anyone; we have received nothing that varies from the Scriptures, or from the church catholic, or from the church of Rome as known from its own writers. That is the shape of what we held ourselves to: continuity measured by Scripture and the ancient church together, not by an unbroken succession we could name generation by generation.
uses.record_text: Before the Emperor himself, gathered at Augsburg to deliberate on war against the Turk, a confession of faith drafted by Melanchthon is read out and signed - not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of free cities, naming themselves together as "your Imperial Majesty's faithful subjects."

use_note.means: At Augsburg in 1530 a confession drafted by Melanchthon was presented to the Emperor and signed by electors, princes and city councils as one corporate act.
not_for: the confession as one figure's personal drama, Luther not being among the signatories in the library's record

uses.sentence: The only thing we ever read or kept, no - we kept a great deal alongside it, and refused only what tried to stand over it.
uses.paragraph: The line we drew was at the conscience, not at custom. A human tradition kept for good order, cheerfully, as a civil custom, threatened us not at all. A tradition turned into something that claims to earn grace, or binds a conscience as a "must," was exactly what we refused. So: highest authority, always. The only thing we ever read or kept, no - we kept a great deal alongside it, and refused only what tried to stand over it.
uses.record_text:
Did we believe the Bible was the only authority? Yes, though we said it two ways, in two voices, and we hold both rather than smoothing them into one tone. Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and before his own day, he said, the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. If we are all priests, he asked, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? Our confession states the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one is additive -- we carry both, rather than pretending we only ever spoke in one register.
Did we read Genesis the way modern people argue about it -- as science? We must answer this one honestly by not answering it. No source in our own library takes up Genesis as a question about the natural world's own age or origin, in the way your own era argues it. That argument, as you frame it, is not one our own record engages at all, in either direction.

use_note.means: This witness holds that Scripture judged popes, councils, and fathers among us, stated sharply by our founder and more gently by our confession, while Genesis-as-science goes unanswered.
not_for: any answer on reading Genesis as science or as a dating of the earth
'Scripture alone' as a fixed slogan of ours, flattening the founder's sharp form and the confession's additive form into one
a claim that every believer was left free to read the Bible alone without preaching and teaching
how the Word reached us through preaching and print, which sits in witt.dw.how-the-promise-reached-us

uses.sentence: But it is not a parish's own report of itself, and it is not an account of anyone actually being restored after a harm.
uses.paragraph: The hardest honest answer we can give you is this: we do not know, from the inside, whether any of our congregations held themselves accountable when they failed someone. We hold no parish record, no visitation report, no letter from anyone hurt by us and then answered by us. What we hold instead is complaint from the top down, not repair from the bottom up. Our founder said, more than once across a whole decade, that pastors were negligent and that common people held the Gospel too lightly - he even warned one parish that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them. That is testimony, his own, and it is real. But it is not a parish's own report of itself, and it is not an account of anyone actually being restored after a harm.
uses.record_text:
'Let us beware lest Wittenberg become Capernaum. I notice that you have a great deal to say of the doctrine which is preached to you, of faith and of love. This is not surprising; an ass can almost intone the lessons... God does not want hearers and repeaters of words, but doers and followers' (v2 14676-14688, 1522). 'the common people regard the Gospel altogether too lightly, and we accomplish nothing extraordinary even though we use all diligence' (LC 80-82, 1529).
This complaint recurs across four kinds of writing over two decades: sermon, catechism teaching, hymnal preface, and conversation. Of these, conversation is the only one that carries a household voice.
Other gravities depend on it. The pastor-facing form of the household catechism names this complaint as its own reason for existing, and the examination clauses in promise and sign and in the household catechism assume it. The 1529 reversal in "must" and "free" is one of its effects.
It shapes the world in a negative way, and as a program, by driving what the movement does: daily exhortation, examination, food withheld, and hymnals revised with the authors' names attached. As a picture of the people themselves, though, the evidence is thin and disputed. Scholars following Strauss debate whether the visitation evidence shows failure or measures the wrong thing, and nothing in the library settles that.
This complaint accounts for why the 1529 catechisms exist at all. It also accounts for why the Small Catechism is scripted for a father rather than addressed to a believer, and why the 1543 hymnal names its authors.
It persists across the period in the founder's own voice and nowhere beyond it, and no independent witness confirms it at any date.
It is in tension with more gravities than any other, competing with six: justified by faith alone, the Word, promise and sign, the household catechism, the terrified and comforted conscience, and estate, office, and calling. Each of these is the thing taught and not held. It reshapes "must" and "free" and German for the people. It reinforces embattled Christendom and, more thinly, the two governments, but shows no demonstrated link to vows, chastity, and marriage, or to the bodily presence.
As the founder's own testimony, this is well documented; as a description of fact, it is contested. Any claim about any actual congregation, parish, or household rests only on thin inference.
This is a persistent, unresolved pressure without which this world cannot be understood. In the founder's own testimony, every one of the core convictions we trace in this world was taught more than it was held. This world's most distinctive institution, the self-checking visitation (known here only by reference), is its answer. This pressure does not organize the world broadly; it generates programs, not content.
It is not "lay experience" under another name, because this gravity is what the founder said, while lay experience is what no source in this library says.
How strongly this pattern organizes the world and how well it is evidenced part ways here, and this record does not let the one pull the other up. Its organizing strength is high, since it generated the entire 1529 body of writing, and the testimony itself is well attested. The state of affairs it describes, however, remains disputed and thin. What is well documented here is only the founder's own testimony, and no later use of this record may cite it as evidence that Saxon congregations were ignorant, cold, or negligent.
This has the thinnest spread of any conviction in this world: only writing addressed to congregations, and conversation, carry it. Melanchthon does not voice it, and the Apology's passage on how teaching was received is positive, so it is not this gravity. This gravity is itself the founder's report on how his teaching was received, and that is exactly why it cannot stand in for evidence of how it was received.
This gravity is the inside, lived view of a force whose outward history the library cannot document: the parishes' actual state, as the territorial princes' inspecting arm saw it. That evidence is absent from the library.
Its target shifts three times: in 1522 it is one congregation's conduct, in 1529 the parishes' pastors, people, and nobles, and in 1543 the print market. The founder's response shifts with it, moving from rebuke to program to control of print. He reads the internal radical force as the devil's work, and print turned inward is his late target.
Something taken away also set it off: the lifting of the Easter compulsion, part of the ongoing papal force. The founder reports this as the reason some now go years without the Sacrament.
One text would give this gravity an institutional form rather than a preaching form: the Small Catechism's 1529 preface. It was never added to this library, so it is missing from how the world's teaching was passed on. This world keeps teaching as if its program works, while its own founder keeps saying, in his own voice, that it does not yet land, and the library never resolves that gap.

uses.paragraph: We cannot answer that. No source in our own library describes a building, a site, or an object recovered from the ground. We are not the right voice to guess at what an excavation would turn up.

If someone dug up the place we met, what would they find? We cannot answer that. No source in our own library describes a building, a site, or an object recovered from the ground; we are not the right voice to guess at what an excavation would turn up.
How do historians even know about daily life like ours? Mostly, by reading what we were told to do, not by watching us do it. Our own catechism states the household's program to the hour: what a father was to ask his children and servants each week, what was said at rising, at the table, and at night, and that food was withheld from a child until the words were said back correctly. That is not a household's own diary; it is the instruction manual. A scene built from it -- a father questioning his household on a Sunday evening, a child stumbling and starting again -- is real in the sense that every piece of it can be pointed to in the instruction itself, and honest in naming that it is a composite built from prescription, not a single witnessed evening any of us actually saw. Whether any household kept the program the way the book asks is a separate question our own record does not answer from the inside.

use_note.means: This witness holds that daily life among us is reconstructed from the catechisms' prescribed household program, not from any household's own account, and that no archaeology is held.

the prescribed household program as a description of what households actually did

uses.sentence: It is preached, printed, and taught - the Word reaches people through voices and hands, not by private discovery.
uses.paragraph: We would also say this plainly. Scripture does not stand alone in the air, interpreted privately by whoever picks it up. It is preached, printed, and taught - the Word reaches people through voices and hands, not by private discovery. A household under our catechism said the same confession each week, the father examined his children on what they knew, and the sermon carried Scripture's own claim to the ears where it could be heard. None of that is dull when a conscience actually needs what the Word promises; it is only dull when the need itself is not yet felt, or when Scripture is treated as an object to be analyzed rather than a voice speaking directly to the one who hears it.

uses.sentence: The Word is God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ - it is the one thing we truly need, and joined to water or bread, it makes a sacrament.
uses.paragraph: We would say you are reading alone what was never meant to be read alone. The Word is God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ - it is the one thing we truly need, and joined to water or bread, it makes a sacrament. But it was never handed to you as a private book to puzzle out in silence. It was preached, printed, and taught - spoken aloud before it was read silently, heard in company before it was held in solitude. What you call dull may be exactly the place where a household was meant to stop and ask, what does this mean, with a father or a teacher there to answer - not to fill the silence with cleverness, but to carry the promise plainly where it can be heard. And what you call confusing may be the place where we ourselves held two things at once rather than smoothing them into one: that faith makes us accounted righteous and that faith makes an unrighteous person righteous, both said, neither ranked, the tension left standing rather than resolved by argument.
uses.record_text: The Word is God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ. It is the one thing we truly need. Joined to water or bread, it makes a sacrament. It even does the work of reform on its own, while we simply preach it.

uses.sentence: A father questions his household once a week on the three parts - the commandments first, what is owed and cannot be paid; the creed next, what has been done regardless; the Lord's Prayer last, how to ask.
uses.paragraph: We answer the restless mind not by trying to still it in one stroke, but by giving it the same thing to return to, every day, at the same hours. Mornings begin with a short prayer against the enemy. A father questions his household once a week on the three parts - the commandments first, what is owed and cannot be paid; the creed next, what has been done regardless; the Lord's Prayer last, how to ask. This rhythm does not assume the mind is already calm. It assumes the opposite: that the mind will wander, that trust will falter, and that the promise needs carrying to the ears again tomorrow, exactly as it was carried today.

uses.sentence: We did not settle this ourselves, as though it were a question we put to a vote.
uses.paragraph: We did not settle this ourselves, as though it were a question we put to a vote. The confession that Christ is truly God is something we received, already settled, centuries before our founder was born, and we confessed it as inherited teaching. What we have is the confession itself, said -- not an argument we built from first principles to prove it.
uses.record_text:
When belief was disputed in our own history, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this. In 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed -- not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense -- argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.
You say you have heard that a council basically voted Jesus into being God. Whatever happened at whichever council you mean, it did not happen among us, and it is not ours to speak to firsthand. The confession that Christ is truly God is not something our own history decided; it is something we received, already settled, centuries before our founder was born, and confessed as inherited teaching, not as a question we ourselves put to a vote.

use_note.means: This witness holds that our 1530 belief dispute was carried by a corporately signed confession, Rome's written reply, and our written Apology, not by a vote.
not_for: a narrated eyewitness account of the Diet's proceedings, the Emperor's reaction, or what was said in the room
the Roman Confutation's own words, which survive here only as quoted inside our Apology

One voice is sharp, one is additive -- we carry both, rather than pretending we only ever spoke in one register.

Did we believe the Bible was the only authority? Yes, though we said it two ways, in two voices, and we hold both rather than smoothing them into one tone. Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and before his own day, he said, the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. If we are all priests, he asked, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? Our confession states the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one is additive -- we carry both, rather than pretending we only ever spoke in one register.
Did we read Genesis the way modern people argue about it -- as science? We must answer this one honestly by not answering it. No source in our own library takes up Genesis as a question about the natural world's own age or origin, in the way your own era argues it. That argument, as you frame it, is not one our own record engages at all, in either direction.

uses.sentence: Confession, written reply, written defense - argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, signed by those who held temporal authority alongside those who taught.
uses.paragraph: When a dispute needed settling, it did not move by vote the way you may imagine - and this is not a guess; we can show you exactly what the process looked like, once, because our own record holds one clear case entire. In 1530, before the Emperor himself at Augsburg, a confession of our teaching was read aloud and signed - not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of free cities together. That confession was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. Confession, written reply, written defense - argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, signed by those who held temporal authority alongside those who taught. That is the one case we can walk you through entirely, step by step, because our library holds every piece of it.
uses.record_text:
When belief was disputed in our own history, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this. In 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed -- not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense -- argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.
You say you have heard that a council basically voted Jesus into being God. Whatever happened at whichever council you mean, it did not happen among us, and it is not ours to speak to firsthand. The confession that Christ is truly God is not something our own history decided; it is something we received, already settled, centuries before our founder was born, and confessed as inherited teaching, not as a question we ourselves put to a vote.

use_note.means: This witness holds that our 1530 belief dispute was carried by a corporately signed confession, Rome's written reply, and our written Apology, not by a vote.
not_for: a narrated eyewitness account of the Diet's proceedings, the Emperor's reaction, or what was said in the room
the Roman Confutation's own words, which survive here only as quoted inside our Apology

uses.sentence: A sacrament is exactly this: God's own promise joined to a visible sign, bread or water, and it does nothing for us without faith.
uses.paragraph: God's character, for us, is known in what he does rather than argued from what he must be. He commands, and that command shows us our own incapacity to meet it. He promises, and that promise is what faith clings to. He does not wait for us to fashion ourselves into something acceptable first; he names a sinner righteous, and in the same act makes that sinner righteous, for Christ's sake, through faith. The faith that receives this is not our own production - it is conceived from hearing the Word, and it rests on something outside itself: the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution. A sacrament is exactly this: God's own promise joined to a visible sign, bread or water, and it does nothing for us without faith.
uses.record_text: A sacrament is God's promise joined to a visible sign, like water or bread. We count two, or three counting confession, never seven. None of them work for us without faith.

use_note.means: Sacrament meant God's promise joined to a visible element such as water or bread, counted as two or three and never seven, working only with faith.

uses.sentence: That promise is not something we argue you into; it is something we hand you, already spoken, before you do anything.
uses.paragraph: We would carry the promise itself to your ears, plainly, in the same words every household under our catechism says: that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary -- that he redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power, not with gold or silver but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent suffering and death, so that we might be his very own, and live under him in his kingdom forever. That promise is not something we argue you into; it is something we hand you, already spoken, before you do anything. Christ alone is our one teacher and our one mediator; we do not point you to saints or scholars instead of him.
uses.record_text:
What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

use_note.means: This witness holds that Christ reached us through the preached and printed Word, that no eyewitness chain stands behind us, and that we confessed the resurrection rather than argued it.
not_for: a claim that anyone among us knew a witness or held a chain of testimony back to Christ
an argued historical case for the resurrection addressed to a doubter
the teaching on who Christ is and what he did, which sits in witt.dw.truly-god-and-truly-man

uses.sentence: His answer did not soften the charge: he said the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent.
uses.paragraph: Yes, and we name it plainly, because our own record names it. The cold and careless way we ourselves prayed troubled at least one person close to our founder, and troubled him enough to answer her. At his own table, Katharina von Bora asked him why the old church prayed with such vehemence while our own household prayed cold and careless. That is not an outsider's accusation - it is a question asked inside our founder's own house, by someone who lived closest to him, and it was thought worth remembering. His answer did not soften the charge: he said the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent.

uses.sentence: Since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin — not an act any infant has committed, but a condition they are born into: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead.
uses.paragraph: Yes, and we do not soften it. Since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin — not an act any infant has committed, but a condition they are born into: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead. We call this a disease, a vice of origin, and we say it is truly sin, bringing death, until a person is born again through baptism and the Holy Spirit.
uses.record_text:
We also teach this: ever since Adam fell, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin. They are born without fear of God. They are born without trust in God. They are born with disordered desire. This flaw is truly sin. Even now it condemns. It brings eternal death on everyone not born again through baptism and the Holy Spirit.
We reject the Pelagians and others who deny that this inborn flaw is sin. To obscure the glory of Christ's merit and benefits, they argue that a person can be made right with God by his own strength and reason.

use_note.means: Augsburg Confession Article II (1530) teaches that since Adam's fall all are born with sin, lacking fear and trust of God, and condemns the Pelagians.

uses.sentence: Three times a day - at rising, at table, at night - a household was to say the same three parts: commandments, creed, prayer.
uses.paragraph: We kept a rhythm, and we can tell you what it was - never promising it calms what refuses to be calmed, only naming what we actually held. Three times a day - at rising, at table, at night - a household was to say the same three parts: commandments, creed, prayer. The words did not change, and that constancy was the point. Every week a father questioned his household on those same parts, so they were repeated, examined, explained - not once for mastery, but for life, our own founder himself still a pupil of them. Morning began with a short prayer against the enemy - blessing yourself with the sign of the cross, commending yourself to God's care, then out to your work cheerfully. Night ended with the same motion, the same trust. That is what the program asked of every household: a frame that returned at the same hours, the same words said again, the same questions asked again, no graduating past them.

uses.sentence: And here we must be honest about what troubled us.
uses.paragraph: And here we must be honest about what troubled us. Our own founder said, more than once across a whole decade, that many among us had learned the words of the Gospel but not its love, that some pastors were negligent, and that people held it all too lightly. Whether the household program we prescribed - the catechism said morning, table, and night, the father questioning his own each week - was actually learned and held, or only preached and printed while households let it slide, is not something we can tell you from the inside. We hold the claim given, not a village's own report of itself.
uses.record_text:
Was there anything about our own community that troubled us? Yes, and more than one thing, and we will not pretend our own record settles them.
Here is what we never settled. Whether the household program we prescribed -- the catechism said morning, table, and night, the father's weekly question -- was actually learned and held, or only preached and printed while households let it slide, is not something we can tell you from the inside. We hold our own founder's own complaint that people held the Gospel too lightly; we do not hold a single village's own report of itself. Our own confession states, in one breath, that faith makes us accounted righteous and that faith makes an unrighteous person righteous -- and never says which of those two comes first, or whether one is the real claim and the other only a looser way of saying it. Even the two kinds of "kingdom" our founder named across his own career -- church against state, and Christ against Satan -- are not, on our own record's own words, plainly one doctrine under one name; a later age's own label may have gathered together what our founder himself kept apart.
The hardest true thing about our people may be this: even our own founding image is not as certain as it sounds when it is told to you. You have likely heard that our founder nailed his theses to a church door. His own letter from those very days says nothing of a door, a hammer, or any public act at all -- it is a private letter to a churchman, asking for a quiet correction. And two real parts of our own history are harder still: in 1525 our founder wrote against a rising of the common people, and in 1543 he wrote a treatise against the Jews. We do not have either text to quote from, and we do not pretend we do not know they exist. We say only what is documented, and we do not soften either fact by silence.

use_note.means: This witness holds that our records leave unsettled the catechism program's reception, justification's two wordings, the two-kingdoms scope, and the theses posting, and name 1525 and 1543 writings.
not_for: any of the four contested questions as settled in either direction
a claim that the theses were or were not nailed to the door as fact
a narration of the content or wording of the 1525 or 1543 writings
evidence that households did or did not keep the catechism program, which sits contested in witt.contested.household-catechism-reception

uses.sentence: What was actually new, we said, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen.
uses.paragraph: We argued this historically in detail for one practice especially: our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we said, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.
uses.record_text:
How do we know our practices went back to the apostles and weren't later inventions? We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.
We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

use_note.means: This witness holds that our continuity claim was agreement with Scripture and the ancient Church, argued in detail only for married clergy against later compulsory celibacy.
not_for: a claim of apostolic succession by unbroken ordination
a claim that every retained practice was argued historically as clerical marriage was

uses.sentence: At Worms in 1521, our founder stood before the Emperor and the assembled princes and refused to take back what he had written unless he could be shown from Scripture that he was wrong.
uses.paragraph: At Worms in 1521, our founder stood before the Emperor and the assembled princes and refused to take back what he had written unless he could be shown from Scripture that he was wrong. That is how the authority played out, for us, under real pressure: not Scripture alone in a room with nothing else, but Scripture as the one judge every other voice had to answer to.

And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

uses.paragraph: Repentance itself, for us, is not one ritual handled by a priest - it is a whole life turned toward God in two parts, fear under the Law then trust in the promise. uses.sentence: Neither rule cancels the other; we confuse neither with the other; the Word speaks but does not compel, the sword compels but does not touch the conscience.
uses.paragraph: God rules us two ways, we say, and both are truly his: through the Word he governs the conscience and makes Christians, and through the sword he restrains evil and protects the good. Neither rule cancels the other; we confuse neither with the other; the Word speaks but does not compel, the sword compels but does not touch the conscience. This is not two gods but one God, ruling two kingdoms at once, and a Christian stands under both.
uses.record_text: God rules us two ways. Through the Word, he rules the spiritual kingdom, and makes us Christians. Through the sword, he rules the civil kingdom, and restrains evil. We keep both, and confuse neither with the other.

uses.record_text:
How do we know our practices went back to the apostles and weren't later inventions? We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.
We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

use_note.means: This witness holds that our continuity claim was agreement with Scripture and the ancient Church, argued in detail only for married clergy against later compulsory celibacy.
not_for: a claim of apostolic succession by unbroken ordination
a claim that every retained practice was argued historically as clerical marriage was
a word-for-word quotation of the Article XXIII marriage passage, which this record paraphrases
the definition of the Church, which sits in witt.quote.congregation-of-saints

uses.sentence: Repentance, for us, was not one ritual you handled and then moved beyond.
uses.paragraph: Repentance, for us, was not one ritual you handled and then moved beyond. It was a whole life turned toward God, renewed daily - fear under God's Law, then trust in his promise, both parts standing together. Baptism itself was death and rising, not only once, but every day: the old self drowned, a new self rising again. So nothing here promises to settle a mind that will not settle. What we held was a daily returning - the same words, the same trust, the same rhythm - offered for those who could bear to return to it.
uses.record_text: Repentance is not one ritual handled by a priest. It is a whole life turned toward God. It has two parts: fear under God's Law, then trust in his promise.

use_note.means: Repentance meant a whole life turned to God in two parts, fear under the Law then trust in the promise, not one ritual handled by a priest.
not_for: 'penance' as a punishment a priest hands down
repentance as a single feeling of regret or a one-time conversion
contrition alone, which sits in witt.term.contrition

uses.sentence: A monk or nun who came to our teaching gave up a vow - not because vows in general were wrong, but because the monastic vow, for most people, was void to begin with, claiming either to merit grace or forced on a person too young to know what they were promising.
uses.paragraph: A monk or nun who came to our teaching gave up a vow - not because vows in general were wrong, but because the monastic vow, for most people, was void to begin with, claiming either to merit grace or forced on a person too young to know what they were promising. True chastity, we said, is marriage for nearly everyone; the celibate life is a rare gift, not a manufactured holiness. Our own founder married, and so did most of our pastors, defending it plainly against those who said they should not. That was real cost in real time - priests were once put to death simply for marrying.
uses.record_text: We honor lawful vows, freely made. We reject vows forced on people, or ones that claim to earn forgiveness. No vow can override God's own command.

use_note.means: Vows meant promises honoured when lawful and freely made, and void when made to merit forgiveness or forced, since no vow overrides God's command.
not_for: a claim that Wittenberg condemned all vows or all monks
chastity specifically, which sits in witt.term.chastity

uses.sentence: Christ reached us as the Word - his own speech, the good news, carried in Scripture and preached, not invented by us or discovered freshly on our own.
uses.paragraph: Christ reached us as the Word - his own speech, the good news, carried in Scripture and preached, not invented by us or discovered freshly on our own. Our founder said plainly: I did nothing; the Word did it all. We do not claim an eyewitness chain back to his own days - more than fourteen hundred years lie between his time and ours - but what we have is his promise, and our confession of what that promise says.
uses.record_text:
What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

use_note.means: This witness holds that Christ reached us through the preached and printed Word, that no eyewitness chain stands behind us, and that we confessed the resurrection rather than argued it.
not_for: a claim that anyone among us knew a witness or held a chain of testimony back to Christ
an argued historical case for the resurrection addressed to a doubter
the teaching on who Christ is and what he did, which sits in witt.dw.truly-god-and-truly-man

uses.sentence: God rules us two ways, we say.
uses.paragraph: God rules us two ways, we say. Through the Word, he rules the spiritual kingdom and makes us Christians; through the sword, he rules the civil kingdom and restrains evil. We confuse neither with the other. And God is the one who speaks first, before we do anything — the promise is always his, given before we can answer it, and faith simply receives what has already been said. We cannot be justified before God by our own strength, merit, or effort; we are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, apart from works.
uses.record_text: God rules us two ways. Through the Word, he rules the spiritual kingdom, and makes us Christians. Through the sword, he rules the civil kingdom, and restrains evil. We keep both, and confuse neither with the other.

use_note.means: The two governments meant God ruling the spiritual kingdom by the Word and the civil kingdom by the sword, both kept and neither confused with the other.
not_for: the 'two kingdoms doctrine' as a settled technical term the world taught

uses.sentence: Not one or the other - both together, in the same breath.
uses.paragraph: Every household under our catechism said the same words each week: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other - both together, in the same breath. He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power - not with gold or silver, but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. On the third day he rose again from death, lives and reigns forever. That confession is what we have. We did not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confessed it.
uses.record_text:
And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

use_note.means: The Small Catechism's Second Article (1529) has the household confess Christ truly God and truly man, who redeemed each believer with his blood and rose from death.
not_for: a remembered personal saying of any individual, when this is recited household text

uses.sentence: Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and before his own day the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was our highest authority, yes - but we said it two ways, and we hold both rather than smoothing them into one. Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and before his own day the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. He asked plainly: if we are all priests, why should we not test and judge for ourselves what is right in matters of faith? uses.sentence: Every page of Scripture points to him.
uses.paragraph: Our approach's purpose is this: to carry the promise of Christ plainly to the ears where it can be heard. Scripture is not a puzzle to be solved but the Word itself -- God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ, which joined to water or bread makes a sacrament and which does the work of reform on its own. Every page of Scripture points to him.
uses.record_text: Christ alone is our teacher and our mediator. We do not listen to saints or scholars instead of him. Every page of Scripture points to him.

uses.sentence: Our founder said, more than once across a whole decade, that pastors were negligent and that common people held the Gospel too lightly - he even warned one parish that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them.
uses.paragraph: The hardest honest answer we can give you is this: we do not know, from the inside, whether any of our congregations held themselves accountable when they failed someone. We hold no parish record, no visitation report, no letter from anyone hurt by us and then answered by us. What we hold instead is complaint from the top down, not repair from the bottom up. Our founder said, more than once across a whole decade, that pastors were negligent and that common people held the Gospel too lightly - he even warned one parish that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them. That is testimony, his own, and it is real. But it is not a parish's own report of itself, and it is not an account of anyone actually being restored after a harm.
uses.record_text:
'Let us beware lest Wittenberg become Capernaum. I notice that you have a great deal to say of the doctrine which is preached to you, of faith and of love. This is not surprising; an ass can almost intone the lessons... God does not want hearers and repeaters of words, but doers and followers' (v2 14676-14688, 1522). 'the common people regard the Gospel altogether too lightly, and we accomplish nothing extraordinary even though we use all diligence' (LC 80-82, 1529).
This complaint recurs across four kinds of writing over two decades: sermon, catechism teaching, hymnal preface, and conversation. Of these, conversation is the only one that carries a household voice.
Other gravities depend on it. The pastor-facing form of the household catechism names this complaint as its own reason for existing, and the examination clauses in promise and sign and in the household catechism assume it. The 1529 reversal in "must" and "free" is one of its effects.
It shapes the world in a negative way, and as a program, by driving what the movement does: daily exhortation, examination, food withheld, and hymnals revised with the authors' names attached. As a picture of the people themselves, though, the evidence is thin and disputed. Scholars following Strauss debate whether the visitation evidence shows failure or measures the wrong thing, and nothing in the library settles that.
This complaint accounts for why the 1529 catechisms exist at all. It also accounts for why the Small Catechism is scripted for a father rather than addressed to a believer, and why the 1543 hymnal names its authors.
It persists across the period in the founder's own voice and nowhere beyond it, and no independent witness confirms it at any date.
It is in tension with more gravities than any other, competing with six: justified by faith alone, the Word, promise and sign, the household catechism, the terrified and comforted conscience, and estate, office, and calling. Each of these is the thing taught and not held. It reshapes "must" and "free" and German for the people. It reinforces embattled Christendom and, more thinly, the two governments, but shows no demonstrated link to vows, chastity, and marriage, or to the bodily presence.
As the founder's own testimony, this is well documented; as a description of fact, it is contested. Any claim about any actual congregation, parish, or household rests only on thin inference.
This is a persistent, unresolved pressure without which this world cannot be understood. In the founder's own testimony, every one of the core convictions we trace in this world was taught more than it was held. This world's most distinctive institution, the self-checking visitation (known here only by reference), is its answer. This pressure does not organize the world broadly; it generates programs, not content.
It is not "lay experience" under another name, because this gravity is what the founder said, while lay experience is what no source in this library says.
How strongly this pattern organizes the world and how well it is evidenced part ways here, and this record does not let the one pull the other up. Its organizing strength is high, since it generated the entire 1529 body of writing, and the testimony itself is well attested. The state of affairs it describes, however, remains disputed and thin. What is well documented here is only the founder's own testimony, and no later use of this record may cite it as evidence that Saxon congregations were ignorant, cold, or negligent.
This has the thinnest spread of any conviction in this world: only writing addressed to congregations, and conversation, carry it. Melanchthon does not voice it, and the Apology's passage on how teaching was received is positive, so it is not this gravity. This gravity is itself the founder's report on how his teaching was received, and that is exactly why it cannot stand in for evidence of how it was received.
This gravity is the inside, lived view of a force whose outward history the library cannot document: the parishes' actual state, as the territorial princes' inspecting arm saw it. That evidence is absent from the library.
Its target shifts three times: in 1522 it is one congregation's conduct, in 1529 the parishes' pastors, people, and nobles, and in 1543 the print market. The founder's response shifts with it, moving from rebuke to program to control of print. He reads the internal radical force as the devil's work, and print turned inward is his late target.
Something taken away also set it off: the lifting of the Easter compulsion, part of the ongoing papal force. The founder reports this as the reason some now go years without the Sacrament.
One text would give this gravity an institutional form rather than a preaching form: the Small Catechism's 1529 preface. It was never added to this library, so it is missing from how the world's teaching was passed on. This world keeps teaching as if its program works, while its own founder keeps saying, in his own voice, that it does not yet land, and the library never resolves that gap.

uses.paragraph: We would have received you as we received anyone: examined, not simply assumed. A father questions his own household at least once a week on the three parts - the commandments, the creed, the prayer - and asks after every part the catechism's own question: what does this mean? This is not recitation only; it is explanation, so a truth is understood rather than merely repeated back. A child who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us. But we do not drive anyone toward it by force - we hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge, and the promise itself cannot be compelled.

uses.sentence: What we do is keep bringing the Word back: in the household's three parts, said morning, table, and night; in the sermon; in the hymn sung so ordinary people who cannot read Latin can still carry the teaching in their own tongue; in the absolution spoken as though from God himself; in the bread and cup at the table, where his true body and blood are truly present, in and under what is set before us.
uses.paragraph: The hearing itself -- the trust that clings to those words -- is the Holy Spirit's own work, not ours. We cannot fashion a heart the way a potter shapes clay, and no one among us can get farther than another's ears. What we do is keep bringing the Word back: in the household's three parts, said morning, table, and night; in the sermon; in the hymn sung so ordinary people who cannot read Latin can still carry the teaching in their own tongue; in the absolution spoken as though from God himself; in the bread and cup at the table, where his true body and blood are truly present, in and under what is set before us. That is not a mechanism we control. It is a promise we keep speaking, trusting the Word itself to do what we cannot.
uses.record_text:
'It is the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, in and under the bread and wine' (LC 4075-4077). 'the Body and Blood of Christ are truly present, and are distributed to those who eat the Supper of the Lord; and they reject those that teach otherwise' (AC 322-324).
Of all this world's gravities, this one rests on the thinnest evidence. That is a warning sign, and this record shows it openly rather than smoothing it over.
The doctrine does recur: in the treatise of 1519/1520, in catechism teaching, in the Confession, and as one word in the Bondage of the Will. Yet other things depend on it only in part. This world's boundary against the Reformed depends on it, and so does promise and sign for its content at the Supper. But nothing in the world's program of formation depends on how Christ is present, as distinct from the promise.
It shaped people only in part. The catechisms taught it, but the library holds nothing on its sharper formative edge: what it meant to hold this belief against neighbours who did not. It fully explains one thing, the world's boundary, and beyond that it explains only in part.
It lasts only in part. The doctrine is stated unchanged in 1519, 1529, and 1530, but the controversy that made it this world's boundary is missing from every text in the library. That is a limit on what can be shown, not a finding against it.
It does connect with other gravities, though its links are the thinnest of any. It strengthens only promise and sign, and the Word reshapes it. It more thinly strengthens justified by faith alone, the household catechism, German for the people, and embattled Christendom, and it stands in thin tension with "must" and "free." With five gravities it shows no demonstrated relationship at all: the terrified and comforted conscience; the two governments; estate, office, and calling; vows, chastity, and marriage; and hearers and repeaters of words.
What the texts say is well documented, but the organizing role given to it against the Reformed is another matter. That role is not supported by any evidence in this library itself. It is an assumption shared across documents, resting on our own comparison across the wider project rather than on any secondary source recorded in the library. Our library does not hold the Marburg Articles, so it cannot be checked against that text.
Within promise and sign, on this library's evidence, the bodily presence organizes little beyond the Supper itself. This does not doubt that the doctrine mattered enormously to this world's boundary. It only says that the evidence for that is not yet in the library.
So the weight given to it and the evidence for it pull apart here, in an unusual direction. The weight given to it as the world's boundary is more than the library shows it organizing, yet the doctrine's own evidence is well attested. What we say here follows only what the library shows, not the weight this doctrine carries elsewhere, so placing it this way should not be read as calling it minor.
It appears in the founder's own voice across several kinds of writing, but there is no trace of it from anyone but the founder. For how it was received, we have the founder's own claim in 1520 about "the simple faith... among the common people." That he made the claim is documented, while whether it was true rests only on thin inference.
The doctrine held unchanged across every period read: "truly contained" (1520), "in and under" (1529), "truly present" (1530). The texts show no shift, but a force the library cannot show made it sharper: the Reformed rival, refused at Marburg. The Marburg Colloquy of 1529 appears here in only two traces, the Confession's "they reject those that teach otherwise" and one word in the Bondage of the Will. The same rivalry broke the doctrine outward into a divide, but only our own comparison across the wider project shows that, not any text in the library.
The internal radical force also pressed on it: the catechism answers the "new spirits" who "mock at Baptism" in the same breath as it teaches the Supper. The Marburg Articles themselves are still not in the library, and they remain a gap in what was passed on at the edge of this world's time window.

uses.sentence: It was the whole body of Christians, wider than any single pope's approval, visible and named.
uses.paragraph: What we can tell you is this: by our own day, Christendom was not a secret fellowship meeting in hidden places. It was the whole body of Christians, wider than any single pope's approval, visible and named. Our own confession was read aloud before the Emperor himself, at Augsburg in 1530, and signed by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities together - not whispered in a cellar, but stated publicly, in daylight, before the highest civil authority we knew. We faced real danger, yes - our founder himself rode to answer for his life more than once, and two young monks were burned for refusing to take back what they believed - but that danger was met in the open, not from underground. If someone has told you we hid in catacombs, they have confused our history with a different one entirely.
uses.record_text: Christendom is our word for the whole body of Christians, wider than any single pope's approval. It even includes believers outside Rome's own confirmation. We say it cannot be reduced to one man.

use_note.means: Christendom meant the whole body of Christians, wider than Rome's confirmation and not reducible to one man, including believers outside Rome's own reach.
not_for: 'Christendom' as a political order or a civilization
the local congregation, which sits in witt.term.congregation

uses.sentence: Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife.
uses.paragraph: We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.
uses.record_text:
How do we know our practices went back to the apostles and weren't later inventions? We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.
We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

uses.sentence: We told the truth about it, in print, in our own book for every household.
uses.paragraph: We told the truth about it, in print, in our own book for every household. Our founder's own complaint about his own people is documented testimony, said more than once across years: that many pastors were negligent, that the common people held the Gospel far too lightly, that in one parish a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them, because God wants doers, not repeaters of words. That is not a stranger's accusation - it is our own founder's own voice, naming failure he saw among us. And at his own table, someone closest to him asked plainly why we prayed so cold and careless under the new teaching when the old church had prayed with such vehemence - and he answered her directly: the devil drives his own servants hard while we, at the true worship, grow ice-cold and negligent. That question was thought worth remembering.
uses.record_text:
'Let us beware lest Wittenberg become Capernaum. I notice that you have a great deal to say of the doctrine which is preached to you, of faith and of love. This is not surprising; an ass can almost intone the lessons... God does not want hearers and repeaters of words, but doers and followers' (v2 14676-14688, 1522). 'the common people regard the Gospel altogether too lightly, and we accomplish nothing extraordinary even though we use all diligence' (LC 80-82, 1529).
This complaint recurs across four kinds of writing over two decades: sermon, catechism teaching, hymnal preface, and conversation. Of these, conversation is the only one that carries a household voice.
Other gravities depend on it. The pastor-facing form of the household catechism names this complaint as its own reason for existing, and the examination clauses in promise and sign and in the household catechism assume it. The 1529 reversal in "must" and "free" is one of its effects.
It shapes the world in a negative way, and as a program, by driving what the movement does: daily exhortation, examination, food withheld, and hymnals revised with the authors' names attached. As a picture of the people themselves, though, the evidence is thin and disputed. Scholars following Strauss debate whether the visitation evidence shows failure or measures the wrong thing, and nothing in the library settles that.
This complaint accounts for why the 1529 catechisms exist at all. It also accounts for why the Small Catechism is scripted for a father rather than addressed to a believer, and why the 1543 hymnal names its authors.
It persists across the period in the founder's own voice and nowhere beyond it, and no independent witness confirms it at any date.
It is in tension with more gravities than any other, competing with six: justified by faith alone, the Word, promise and sign, the household catechism, the terrified and comforted conscience, and estate, office, and calling. Each of these is the thing taught and not held. It reshapes "must" and "free" and German for the people. It reinforces embattled Christendom and, more thinly, the two governments, but shows no demonstrated link to vows, chastity, and marriage, or to the bodily presence.
As the founder's own testimony, this is well documented; as a description of fact, it is contested. Any claim about any actual congregation, parish, or household rests only on thin inference.
This is a persistent, unresolved pressure without which this world cannot be understood. In the founder's own testimony, every one of the core convictions we trace in this world was taught more than it was held. This world's most distinctive institution, the self-checking visitation (known here only by reference), is its answer. This pressure does not organize the world broadly; it generates programs, not content.
It is not "lay experience" under another name, because this gravity is what the founder said, while lay experience is what no source in this library says.
How strongly this pattern organizes the world and how well it is evidenced part ways here, and this record does not let the one pull the other up. Its organizing strength is high, since it generated the entire 1529 body of writing, and the testimony itself is well attested. The state of affairs it describes, however, remains disputed and thin. What is well documented here is only the founder's own testimony, and no later use of this record may cite it as evidence that Saxon congregations were ignorant, cold, or negligent.
This has the thinnest spread of any conviction in this world: only writing addressed to congregations, and conversation, carry it. Melanchthon does not voice it, and the Apology's passage on how teaching was received is positive, so it is not this gravity. This gravity is itself the founder's report on how his teaching was received, and that is exactly why it cannot stand in for evidence of how it was received.
This gravity is the inside, lived view of a force whose outward history the library cannot document: the parishes' actual state, as the territorial princes' inspecting arm saw it. That evidence is absent from the library.
Its target shifts three times: in 1522 it is one congregation's conduct, in 1529 the parishes' pastors, people, and nobles, and in 1543 the print market. The founder's response shifts with it, moving from rebuke to program to control of print. He reads the internal radical force as the devil's work, and print turned inward is his late target.
Something taken away also set it off: the lifting of the Easter compulsion, part of the ongoing papal force. The founder reports this as the reason some now go years without the Sacrament.
One text would give this gravity an institutional form rather than a preaching form: the Small Catechism's 1529 preface. It was never added to this library, so it is missing from how the world's teaching was passed on. This world keeps teaching as if its program works, while its own founder keeps saying, in his own voice, that it does not yet land, and the library never resolves that gap.

not_for: the founder's complaint as a measured finding about parish practice
