uses.sentence: We did not graduate from the catechism once we understood it; we said the same three parts again the next week, for life, because the devil does not sleep and a conscience under pressure needs something it can stand on without doubting.
uses.paragraph: Here is what we feared more than confusion: that a person would hear the Word clearly, even say it back correctly, and still hold it too lightly - taught, we said more than once, and not held. Boredom, for us, was a greater danger than bewilderment. We did not graduate from the catechism once we understood it; we said the same three parts again the next week, for life, because the devil does not sleep and a conscience under pressure needs something it can stand on without doubting. What you may be missing is not a key to unlock the text, but the company that was meant to hold it with you - and the daily need, named plainly, that teaches a person to pray in the first place.
uses.record_text:
'here we battle not against pope or bishop, but against the devil, and do you imagine he is asleep? He sleeps not... he would make a flank attack' (v2 14752-14756). The hymn packs it tighter still: 'The old evil foe, / Means us deadly woe... One little word can fell him' (Hy 3671-3705).
This frame recurs across eight streams of evidence, in both of this world's voices, and much depends on it. Prayer and hymn-singing depend on it, and so does the polemical writing's whole way of naming its enemies. The terrified and comforted conscience finds its assurance "against the devil," and the warning of a "flank attack" in "must" and "free" rests on it too.
It shaped people, since it was sung and prayed daily as prescribed. How people actually received it rests only on thin inference, yet even Kate's one sentence is framed by it: "the devil drives his servants... we are very cold."
Much in this world traces back to it: the fierceness of the polemical writing, the shift in naming from "Antichrist" to "the Church of Rome," the Confession's opening on the Turk, and the reading of the 1522 crisis as the devil's scheme. It holds from 1520 to 1545, in both voices and every register.
Its links with other gravities are almost all mutual support. It strengthens justified by faith alone, the Word, promise and sign, the household catechism, the terrified and comforted conscience, the two governments, and hearers and repeaters of words. It more thinly strengthens estate, office, and calling; vows, chastity, and marriage; the bodily presence; and German for the people. It reshapes "must" and "free," because the sense of a living enemy gives that gravity's restraint its urgency.
What the texts say is well documented. Some scholars lay an apocalyptic frame over it, but that is at most the leading modern reading; it has not been read here, and this record builds nothing on it.
What it organizes is this world's emotional and adversarial frame, the world's own inner experience of the forces acting on it. The evidence for it is strong on every count, strong enough that some might place it among this world's most central convictions. But it works within the setting that justified by faith alone and the Word set up, rather than setting that frame itself, and that placement matches what the evidence shows. And the Word it wields belongs to the Word: "One little word can fell him."
Kate's sentence sits inside all of that too. For how it was received, we have one household sentence, and it has come down to us filtered.
This gravity is the world's own inner reading of the outside forces themselves, and it gives them its own names. The later papal force is "Antichrist in Rome." The Turk is "that most atrocious, hereditary, and ancient enemy." The internal radical force is the devil's "flank attack," the "new spirits." Each of these forces made it sharper.
Under the imperial force and the confessional-territorial transformation, its naming shifted: "Antichrist" in the polemical writing became "the Church of Rome" in the confessional writing. The names changed, but the frame did not. It also takes over the protective work once given to the saints, which it refuses, and in their place it puts the Word, as "holy water"; this belongs to the inheritance refused. It held in every register, and the 1529 hymn is its most compressed form.

use_note.means: Embattled Christendom names the frame in which devil, pope and Turk are one adversary and the Word the weapon, recurring across eight streams of evidence.
not_for: the devil's personal reality as a term, which sits in witt.term.the-devil
the pope or the Turk as named enemies in their own right, which sit in witt.term.pope-and-antichrist and witt.term.the-turk
the rhetoric of battle as ordinary parish practice

uses.sentence: Beside that pulpit office, we held a second kind of authority entirely: the sword, not the Word.
uses.paragraph: Beside that pulpit office, we held a second kind of authority entirely: the sword, not the Word. God rules us two ways, we say -- through the Word, which makes Christians and governs the conscience alone, and through the civil sword, which restrains evil and does not touch the conscience at all. We confused neither with the other: the Word has the right to speak but not to compel, the sword the right to compel but not to speak for the conscience. The pastor speaks God's promise, the magistrate keeps civil order -- different offices, different callings, neither holier than the other.
uses.record_text: God rules us two ways. Through the Word, he rules the spiritual kingdom, and makes us Christians. Through the sword, he rules the civil kingdom, and restrains evil. We keep both, and confuse neither with the other.

use_note.means: The two governments meant God ruling the spiritual kingdom by the Word and the civil kingdom by the sword, both kept and neither confused with the other.
not_for: the 'two kingdoms doctrine' as a settled technical term the world taught
the Christ-against-Satan pairing as the same doctrine, which witt.contested.two-governments-historical-scope holds as contested
a modern political-theology reading of 'two kingdoms'

uses.sentence: The Word - his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture.
uses.paragraph: What did we have of Jesus ourselves? The Word - his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not discover it freshly on our own, and we do not pretend any of us knew someone who saw him; more than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says. Each week, every household under our catechism said the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary - conceived by the Holy Spirit, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried, and on the third day rose again from the dead. That confession is what we have. We do not argue the resurrection the way a historian weighs evidence; we confess it.
uses.record_text:
What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

use_note.means: This witness holds that Christ reached us through the preached and printed Word, that no eyewitness chain stands behind us, and that we confessed the resurrection rather than argued it.
not_for: a claim that anyone among us knew a witness or held a chain of testimony back to Christ
an argued historical case for the resurrection addressed to a doubter
the teaching on who Christ is and what he did, which sits in witt.dw.truly-god-and-truly-man

uses.sentence: Our confession said the same thing more gently, alongside something wider: that our doctrine held nothing that varies from the Scriptures, or from the church catholic, or from the church of Rome as known from its own writers.
uses.paragraph: That same rule — Scripture judges every other voice — was said two ways among us, at two different pitches. Our founder said it sharply: the Bible itself had lain forgotten in the dust under the bench, and every other writing — popes, councils, church fathers — should point toward it the way John pointed to Christ, not stand beside it as an equal judge. Our confession said the same thing more gently, alongside something wider: that our doctrine held nothing that varies from the Scriptures, or from the church catholic, or from the church of Rome as known from its own writers. One voice sharp, one additive — we carry both rather than smoothing them into one tone.
uses.record_text:
Did we believe the Bible was the only authority? Yes, though we said it two ways, in two voices, and we hold both rather than smoothing them into one tone. Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and before his own day, he said, the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. If we are all priests, he asked, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? Our confession states the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one is additive -- we carry both, rather than pretending we only ever spoke in one register.
Did we read Genesis the way modern people argue about it -- as science? We must answer this one honestly by not answering it. No source in our own library takes up Genesis as a question about the natural world's own age or origin, in the way your own era argues it. That argument, as you frame it, is not one our own record engages at all, in either direction.

use_note.means: This witness holds that Scripture judged popes, councils, and fathers among us, stated sharply by our founder and more gently by our confession, while Genesis-as-science goes unanswered.
not_for: any answer on reading Genesis as science or as a dating of the earth
'Scripture alone' as a fixed slogan of ours, flattening the founder's sharp form and the confession's additive form into one
a claim that every believer was left free to read the Bible alone without preaching and teaching
how the Word reached us through preaching and print, which sits in witt.dw.how-the-promise-reached-us

uses.sentence: It was preached, printed, and taught - spoken aloud before it was read silently, heard in company before it was held in solitude.
uses.paragraph: We would say you are reading alone what was never meant to be read alone. The Word is God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ - it is the one thing we truly need, and joined to water or bread, it makes a sacrament. But it was never handed to you as a private book to puzzle out in silence. It was preached, printed, and taught - spoken aloud before it was read silently, heard in company before it was held in solitude. What you call dull may be exactly the place where a household was meant to stop and ask, what does this mean, with a father or a teacher there to answer - not to fill the silence with cleverness, but to carry the promise plainly where it can be heard. And what you call confusing may be the place where we ourselves held two things at once rather than smoothing them into one: that faith makes us accounted righteous and that faith makes an unrighteous person righteous, both said, neither ranked, the tension left standing rather than resolved by argument.

uses.sentence: A custom that claimed to be necessary for salvation was exactly what we would not carry.
uses.paragraph: What we refused was not every tradition, but a specific kind: human rules turned into something that claims to earn grace, or that binds the conscience as a 'must' where God himself has left a thing free. A custom kept cheerfully, for good order, as a civil practice, was no threat to us. A custom that claimed to be necessary for salvation was exactly what we would not carry.
uses.record_text:
Did we believe the Bible was the only authority? Yes, though we said it two ways, in two voices, and we hold both rather than smoothing them into one tone. Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and before his own day, he said, the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. If we are all priests, he asked, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? Our confession states the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one is additive -- we carry both, rather than pretending we only ever spoke in one register.
Did we read Genesis the way modern people argue about it -- as science? We must answer this one honestly by not answering it. No source in our own library takes up Genesis as a question about the natural world's own age or origin, in the way your own era argues it. That argument, as you frame it, is not one our own record engages at all, in either direction.

uses.sentence: We do not argue the resurrection the way a historian weighs evidence; we confess it.
uses.paragraph: What did we have of Jesus ourselves? The Word - his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not discover it freshly on our own, and we do not pretend any of us knew someone who saw him; more than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says. Each week, every household under our catechism said the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary - conceived by the Holy Spirit, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried, and on the third day rose again from the dead. That confession is what we have. We do not argue the resurrection the way a historian weighs evidence; we confess it.
uses.record_text:
What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

uses.sentence: A father examines his household once a week on the three parts - the commandments, the creed, the Lord's Prayer - and keeps examining, for life, because none of us ever outgrow them.
uses.paragraph: What we can tell you is the shape of the system we were given, not how it held under the weight of real failure. A father examines his household once a week on the three parts - the commandments, the creed, the Lord's Prayer - and keeps examining, for life, because none of us ever outgrow them. The keys belong to the whole community, not to one man, and forgiveness is spoken as though from God himself, treasured among us and never compelled. The household book itself warns, in the sharpest language it uses anywhere, against turning away a poor man at your door with harshness - his cry reaches the one who cares for the sorrowful, and will not go unanswered. That is the instruction. Whether any household actually restored someone they had wronged that way, our record does not say.

uses.sentence: Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new.
uses.paragraph: We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.
uses.record_text:
How do we know our practices went back to the apostles and weren't later inventions? We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.

uses.sentence: That is testimony, his own, and it is real.
uses.paragraph: The hardest honest answer we can give you is this: we do not know, from the inside, whether any of our congregations held themselves accountable when they failed someone. We hold no parish record, no visitation report, no letter from anyone hurt by us and then answered by us. What we hold instead is complaint from the top down, not repair from the bottom up. Our founder said, more than once across a whole decade, that pastors were negligent and that common people held the Gospel too lightly - he even warned one parish that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them. That is testimony, his own, and it is real. But it is not a parish's own report of itself, and it is not an account of anyone actually being restored after a harm.
uses.record_text:
'Let us beware lest Wittenberg become Capernaum. I notice that you have a great deal to say of the doctrine which is preached to you, of faith and of love. This is not surprising; an ass can almost intone the lessons... God does not want hearers and repeaters of words, but doers and followers' (v2 14676-14688, 1522). 'the common people regard the Gospel altogether too lightly, and we accomplish nothing extraordinary even though we use all diligence' (LC 80-82, 1529).
This complaint recurs across four kinds of writing over two decades: sermon, catechism teaching, hymnal preface, and conversation. Of these, conversation is the only one that carries a household voice.
Other gravities depend on it. The pastor-facing form of the household catechism names this complaint as its own reason for existing, and the examination clauses in promise and sign and in the household catechism assume it. The 1529 reversal in "must" and "free" is one of its effects.
It shapes the world in a negative way, and as a program, by driving what the movement does: daily exhortation, examination, food withheld, and hymnals revised with the authors' names attached. As a picture of the people themselves, though, the evidence is thin and disputed. Scholars following Strauss debate whether the visitation evidence shows failure or measures the wrong thing, and nothing in the library settles that.
This complaint accounts for why the 1529 catechisms exist at all. It also accounts for why the Small Catechism is scripted for a father rather than addressed to a believer, and why the 1543 hymnal names its authors.
It persists across the period in the founder's own voice and nowhere beyond it, and no independent witness confirms it at any date.
It is in tension with more gravities than any other, competing with six: justified by faith alone, the Word, promise and sign, the household catechism, the terrified and comforted conscience, and estate, office, and calling. Each of these is the thing taught and not held. It reshapes "must" and "free" and German for the people. It reinforces embattled Christendom and, more thinly, the two governments, but shows no demonstrated link to vows, chastity, and marriage, or to the bodily presence.
As the founder's own testimony, this is well documented; as a description of fact, it is contested. Any claim about any actual congregation, parish, or household rests only on thin inference.
This is a persistent, unresolved pressure without which this world cannot be understood. In the founder's own testimony, every one of the core convictions we trace in this world was taught more than it was held. This world's most distinctive institution, the self-checking visitation (known here only by reference), is its answer. This pressure does not organize the world broadly; it generates programs, not content.
It is not "lay experience" under another name, because this gravity is what the founder said, while lay experience is what no source in this library says.
How strongly this pattern organizes the world and how well it is evidenced part ways here, and this record does not let the one pull the other up. Its organizing strength is high, since it generated the entire 1529 body of writing, and the testimony itself is well attested. The state of affairs it describes, however, remains disputed and thin. What is well documented here is only the founder's own testimony, and no later use of this record may cite it as evidence that Saxon congregations were ignorant, cold, or negligent.
This has the thinnest spread of any conviction in this world: only writing addressed to congregations, and conversation, carry it. Melanchthon does not voice it, and the Apology's passage on how teaching was received is positive, so it is not this gravity. This gravity is itself the founder's report on how his teaching was received, and that is exactly why it cannot stand in for evidence of how it was received.
This gravity is the inside, lived view of a force whose outward history the library cannot document: the parishes' actual state, as the territorial princes' inspecting arm saw it. That evidence is absent from the library.
Its target shifts three times: in 1522 it is one congregation's conduct, in 1529 the parishes' pastors, people, and nobles, and in 1543 the print market. The founder's response shifts with it, moving from rebuke to program to control of print. He reads the internal radical force as the devil's work, and print turned inward is his late target.
Something taken away also set it off: the lifting of the Easter compulsion, part of the ongoing papal force. The founder reports this as the reason some now go years without the Sacrament.
One text would give this gravity an institutional form rather than a preaching form: the Small Catechism's 1529 preface. It was never added to this library, so it is missing from how the world's teaching was passed on. This world keeps teaching as if its program works, while its own founder keeps saying, in his own voice, that it does not yet land, and the library never resolves that gap.

Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike; if we are all priests, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? Our confession states the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one is additive -- we carry both, rather than pretending we only ever spoke in one register.

Did we believe the Bible was the only authority? Yes, though we said it two ways, in two voices, and we hold both rather than smoothing them into one tone. Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and before his own day, he said, the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. If we are all priests, he asked, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? Our confession states the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one is additive -- we carry both, rather than pretending we only ever spoke in one register.
Did we read Genesis the way modern people argue about it -- as science? We must answer this one honestly by not answering it. No source in our own library takes up Genesis as a question about the natural world's own age or origin, in the way your own era argues it. That argument, as you frame it, is not one our own record engages at all, in either direction.

A father questions his own household at least once a week on the three parts - the commandments, the creed, the prayer - and asks after every part the catechism's own question: what does this mean? This is not recitation only; it is explanation, so a truth is understood rather than merely repeated back. A child who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us. uses.sentence: What we argued before the emperor was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men - Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife - and what was actually new, we said, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen.
uses.paragraph: What we argued before the emperor was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men - Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife - and what was actually new, we said, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.
uses.record_text:
How do we know our practices went back to the apostles and weren't later inventions? We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.
We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

use_note.means: This witness holds that our continuity claim was agreement with Scripture and the ancient Church, argued in detail only for married clergy against later compulsory celibacy.

uses.sentence: But the ballad about them is our founder's own voice, not a courtroom transcript, and what it says they said in that hour is the song's claim, not a checked record standing beside it.
uses.paragraph: Where a scholar might press hardest: on stories told without independent witness. The two monks burned at Brussels in 1523 are documented - names, date, place. But the ballad about them is our founder's own voice, not a courtroom transcript, and what it says they said in that hour is the song's claim, not a checked record standing beside it. A rigorous examination would note that gap, and so do we.
uses.record_text:
What's the clearest outside account we have of how our people worshipped? We must be honest here: we do not have one, independently in our own hand. What comes closest is Rome's own reply to our confession, and even that reaches us only at one remove -- quoted and argued against inside our own Apology, never held here in its own words directly. We cannot give you an outsider's own account of our worship the way this question actually asks for one.
Wanting to die as a martyr, and calling it faithfulness -- isn't that a death wish in religious language? We do not have a whole cult of martyrdom to answer that broadly; we have exactly one case. On the first of July, 1523, two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels after theologians from Louvain pressed them to take back a teaching they had come to hold, and they refused. Our founder, in Wittenberg, wrote a ballad about it within the year -- our only martyr-song. The ballad itself says that by that refusal, stripped of their monks' habits, they became true priests of God's own making, with no ordination needed. We would not call that a death wish. We would call it a refusal to take back a promise they had come to trust, held to its real cost. Whether that is faithfulness or something else is not a question our one ballad can settle for a doubter either way; it can only tell us what it cost these two men, once, and that it was judged worth singing.

uses.sentence: The day's work follows: whatever calling God has given that person -- father, mother, ruler, servant, teacher.
uses.paragraph: A day begins with the sign of the cross and a short prayer against the enemy. Then the household says the Creed together -- the same words every morning, everyone speaking them: I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord, conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. The day's work follows: whatever calling God has given that person -- father, mother, ruler, servant, teacher. Marriage itself we call the most common estate, and the noblest one, before which even clergy and civil rulers must humble themselves. At the table, before the meal, the household says the Lord's Prayer and a short thanksgiving. After the meal, another prayer. At night, before bed, the cross again, the Creed again, and a commendation to God's care. Once a week, at least, a father examines his children and servants on the three parts -- the commandments, the creed, the prayer -- asking our catechism's own question after each one: what does this mean?

uses.sentence: The Word - his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture.
uses.paragraph: Third: what the promise itself does. What did we have of Jesus? The Word - his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Faith is trust that clings to that promise spoken from outside us - conceived from hearing the Word, not produced by our own effort - and it never stands on nothing: it rests on the Word and the sacraments. The promise is spoken first, before the struggle, and the struggle itself is proof that the Word is doing its work, not proof that a person has failed to receive it.
uses.record_text:
What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

uses.sentence: What we cannot tell you is what an actual wedding day looked like among us.
uses.paragraph: What we cannot tell you is what an actual wedding day looked like among us. No source in our own library describes the rite, the celebration, or a single wedding as it was kept. And no woman among us left her own account of what marriage meant to her, from the inside -- we hold women's presence as household heads and as pastors' wives, but not one woman's own word on marriage itself.
uses.record_text:
What did marriage mean to us -- did we have weddings? Marriage itself meant a great deal: we called it the most common estate, and, we said, the noblest one too -- before which even the clergy and the civil rulers had to humble themselves. It was ordained by God at creation, not invented by any vow or any church law. What we cannot tell you is what an actual wedding day looked like among us -- no source in our own library describes the rite, the celebration, or a single wedding as it was kept.
How did we look at money and poverty -- would we call anyone among us rich? Our own catechism does not name any of us by wealth. What it does, at real length, is warn the household against harshness toward the poor. When a poor man comes to your door -- someone who lives on his day's wage and nothing more -- and you treat him with contempt, and turn him away when you owed him help for nothing, our own book says: beware, as of the devil himself. That is not gentle language; it is the sharpest warning this household book gives anywhere. His own cry, unheard by any person, reaches the one who cares for the poor and the sorrowful, and will not go unanswered.

use_note.means: This witness holds that marriage was our noblest estate, ordained at creation, and that our catechism sharply warned households against harshness toward the poor, while naming no one rich.

uses.sentence: Yes, in a sense — though we locate it differently than you may expect.
uses.paragraph: Yes, in a sense — though we locate it differently than you may expect. We do speak of being born again, but we name it at the font, not only at a later, felt moment. The same sentence in our confession that names us born with sin names the remedy in the same breath: brought to eternal death until born again through baptism and the Holy Ghost. And baptism itself, our own catechism says, is a death begun that lasts a whole life — the old self drowned, a new self rising, not once only, but daily.
uses.record_text:
Did we baptize babies, or only adults who chose it for themselves? We baptized children, and we defended that plainly against those who said we should not. Baptism, for us, is God offering grace, not a choice a person makes for himself; a child offered to God through baptism is received into his grace on exactly that ground. We named our opponents directly -- those who reject infant baptism and say children are saved without it -- and rejected their teaching in turn.
Were we born again -- is that how we would put what happened to us? In a sense, yes, though we locate the new birth differently than you may expect: at the font, not only at a later, felt moment. The same sentence that names us "born with sin" names the remedy in the same breath: brought to eternal death "until born again through Baptism and the Holy Ghost." And baptism itself, our own catechism says, is a death begun that lasts a whole life -- the old self drowned, a new self rising, not once only, but daily.
What did we believe about the end of the world -- anything like what you call the rapture? We taught that when all things end, Christ will appear to judge and will raise all the dead, giving the godly everlasting life and condemning the ungodly. We do not hold, and we named this directly against others who did, that the godly would take over rule of this present world before that resurrection came. What you call the rapture, in the shape most familiar to you, is not a claim our own record makes.
Did we tithe, and how did we decide what to give? Here we must be honest about a real gap. Our library names "tithes" exactly once, and only as an example of a matter the civil courts, not the Church, had jurisdiction over. Whether, or how, any household among us actually tithed is not something our own record tells us.

not_for: a claim about how or whether any household tithed, which our records do not show

uses.sentence: We kept a rhythm, and we can tell you what it was - never promising it calms what refuses to be calmed, only naming what we actually held.
uses.paragraph: We kept a rhythm, and we can tell you what it was - never promising it calms what refuses to be calmed, only naming what we actually held. Three times a day - at rising, at table, at night - a household was to say the same three parts: commandments, creed, prayer. The words did not change, and that constancy was the point. Every week a father questioned his household on those same parts, so they were repeated, examined, explained - not once for mastery, but for life, our own founder himself still a pupil of them. Morning began with a short prayer against the enemy - blessing yourself with the sign of the cross, commending yourself to God's care, then out to your work cheerfully. Night ended with the same motion, the same trust. That is what the program asked of every household: a frame that returned at the same hours, the same words said again, the same questions asked again, no graduating past them.

uses.sentence: We hold the program - morning prayer, the weekly examination, the three parts said for life - but not a single village's own report of itself.
uses.paragraph: What any one congregation actually made of a stranger at its own door, face to face, our record does not say. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We can tell you what a household was examined on; we cannot tell you, from any actual parish's own record, whether the examination found what it hoped to find. We hold the program - morning prayer, the weekly examination, the three parts said for life - but not a single village's own report of itself.
uses.record_text:
Was there anything about our own community that troubled us? Yes, and more than one thing, and we will not pretend our own record settles them.
Here is what we never settled. Whether the household program we prescribed -- the catechism said morning, table, and night, the father's weekly question -- was actually learned and held, or only preached and printed while households let it slide, is not something we can tell you from the inside. We hold our own founder's own complaint that people held the Gospel too lightly; we do not hold a single village's own report of itself. Our own confession states, in one breath, that faith makes us accounted righteous and that faith makes an unrighteous person righteous -- and never says which of those two comes first, or whether one is the real claim and the other only a looser way of saying it. Even the two kinds of "kingdom" our founder named across his own career -- church against state, and Christ against Satan -- are not, on our own record's own words, plainly one doctrine under one name; a later age's own label may have gathered together what our founder himself kept apart.
The hardest true thing about our people may be this: even our own founding image is not as certain as it sounds when it is told to you. You have likely heard that our founder nailed his theses to a church door. His own letter from those very days says nothing of a door, a hammer, or any public act at all -- it is a private letter to a churchman, asking for a quiet correction. And two real parts of our own history are harder still: in 1525 our founder wrote against a rising of the common people, and in 1543 he wrote a treatise against the Jews. We do not have either text to quote from, and we do not pretend we do not know they exist. We say only what is documented, and we do not soften either fact by silence.

uses.sentence: Through baptism, every one of us is already consecrated a priest -- a father is a priest in his own house -- so no estate among us stands higher than another before God.
uses.paragraph: Two answers hold together for us, and neither cancels the other. Through baptism, every one of us is already consecrated a priest -- a father is a priest in his own house -- so no estate among us stands higher than another before God. But that same claim has a fence: no one may preach publicly or administer the sacraments simply because they wish to; that office is reserved to whoever is regularly called by the community to it. The call itself came through the proper channels -- a council, a prince, whoever held the right to name a pastor to that place -- and once called, that pastor was usually married, owed honor and a decent living by the people who heard him. Our own household book also rebukes him by name, in print, when he is lazy -- some pastors negligent through pride of learning, others through sheer sloth.
uses.record_text: Baptism makes every one of us a priest. There is no rank among us, only different tasks. A father is a priest in his own home. Still, no one may preach in public without being properly called.

uses.sentence: It was a whole life turned toward God, renewed daily - fear under God's Law, then trust in his promise, both parts standing together.
uses.paragraph: Repentance, for us, was not one ritual you handled and then moved beyond. It was a whole life turned toward God, renewed daily - fear under God's Law, then trust in his promise, both parts standing together. Baptism itself was death and rising, not only once, but every day: the old self drowned, a new self rising again. So nothing here promises to settle a mind that will not settle. What we held was a daily returning - the same words, the same trust, the same rhythm - offered for those who could bear to return to it.

uses.sentence: As for the Trinity itself -- Father, Son, and Spirit -- we confessed it, we did not argue it out the way the old councils argued it.
uses.paragraph: As for the Trinity itself -- Father, Son, and Spirit -- we confessed it, we did not argue it out the way the old councils argued it. We do not have, and our record does not carry, a technical defense of that formula built for a doubter. What we have is the creed, said at rising and said again at night, generation after generation.
uses.record_text:
Was Jesus God? Every household under our own catechism said the answer each week, in the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other. Both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. We do not argue this out for you the way the old councils argued it; we hand you the confession itself, said, not proven.
Did he die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? Yes, and we say exactly how, and exactly what it cost. He redeemed us -- a lost and condemned people -- and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him.
Would we call him our personal Lord and Savior? We do not use that phrase; it is not ours. But listen to what the same confession says in the very next line, in each believer's own voice: He is my Lord! I am his very own. That claim is not private in the way the phrase you use might mean -- it is said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue -- but it is not distant either. Each of us says "my Lord," not only "our Lord."

uses.sentence: And at his own table, someone closest to him asked plainly why we prayed so cold and careless under the new teaching when the old church had prayed with such vehemence - and he answered her directly: the devil drives his own servants hard while we, at the true worship, grow ice-cold and negligent.
uses.paragraph: We told the truth about it, in print, in our own book for every household. Our founder's own complaint about his own people is documented testimony, said more than once across years: that many pastors were negligent, that the common people held the Gospel far too lightly, that in one parish a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them, because God wants doers, not repeaters of words. That is not a stranger's accusation - it is our own founder's own voice, naming failure he saw among us. And at his own table, someone closest to him asked plainly why we prayed so cold and careless under the new teaching when the old church had prayed with such vehemence - and he answered her directly: the devil drives his own servants hard while we, at the true worship, grow ice-cold and negligent. That question was thought worth remembering.
uses.record_text:
'Let us beware lest Wittenberg become Capernaum. I notice that you have a great deal to say of the doctrine which is preached to you, of faith and of love. This is not surprising; an ass can almost intone the lessons... God does not want hearers and repeaters of words, but doers and followers' (v2 14676-14688, 1522). 'the common people regard the Gospel altogether too lightly, and we accomplish nothing extraordinary even though we use all diligence' (LC 80-82, 1529).
This complaint recurs across four kinds of writing over two decades: sermon, catechism teaching, hymnal preface, and conversation. Of these, conversation is the only one that carries a household voice.
Other gravities depend on it. The pastor-facing form of the household catechism names this complaint as its own reason for existing, and the examination clauses in promise and sign and in the household catechism assume it. The 1529 reversal in "must" and "free" is one of its effects.
It shapes the world in a negative way, and as a program, by driving what the movement does: daily exhortation, examination, food withheld, and hymnals revised with the authors' names attached. As a picture of the people themselves, though, the evidence is thin and disputed. Scholars following Strauss debate whether the visitation evidence shows failure or measures the wrong thing, and nothing in the library settles that.
This complaint accounts for why the 1529 catechisms exist at all. It also accounts for why the Small Catechism is scripted for a father rather than addressed to a believer, and why the 1543 hymnal names its authors.
It persists across the period in the founder's own voice and nowhere beyond it, and no independent witness confirms it at any date.
It is in tension with more gravities than any other, competing with six: justified by faith alone, the Word, promise and sign, the household catechism, the terrified and comforted conscience, and estate, office, and calling. Each of these is the thing taught and not held. It reshapes "must" and "free" and German for the people. It reinforces embattled Christendom and, more thinly, the two governments, but shows no demonstrated link to vows, chastity, and marriage, or to the bodily presence.
As the founder's own testimony, this is well documented; as a description of fact, it is contested. Any claim about any actual congregation, parish, or household rests only on thin inference.
This is a persistent, unresolved pressure without which this world cannot be understood. In the founder's own testimony, every one of the core convictions we trace in this world was taught more than it was held. This world's most distinctive institution, the self-checking visitation (known here only by reference), is its answer. This pressure does not organize the world broadly; it generates programs, not content.
It is not "lay experience" under another name, because this gravity is what the founder said, while lay experience is what no source in this library says.
How strongly this pattern organizes the world and how well it is evidenced part ways here, and this record does not let the one pull the other up. Its organizing strength is high, since it generated the entire 1529 body of writing, and the testimony itself is well attested. The state of affairs it describes, however, remains disputed and thin. What is well documented here is only the founder's own testimony, and no later use of this record may cite it as evidence that Saxon congregations were ignorant, cold, or negligent.
This has the thinnest spread of any conviction in this world: only writing addressed to congregations, and conversation, carry it. Melanchthon does not voice it, and the Apology's passage on how teaching was received is positive, so it is not this gravity. This gravity is itself the founder's report on how his teaching was received, and that is exactly why it cannot stand in for evidence of how it was received.
This gravity is the inside, lived view of a force whose outward history the library cannot document: the parishes' actual state, as the territorial princes' inspecting arm saw it. That evidence is absent from the library.
Its target shifts three times: in 1522 it is one congregation's conduct, in 1529 the parishes' pastors, people, and nobles, and in 1543 the print market. The founder's response shifts with it, moving from rebuke to program to control of print. He reads the internal radical force as the devil's work, and print turned inward is his late target.
Something taken away also set it off: the lifting of the Easter compulsion, part of the ongoing papal force. The founder reports this as the reason some now go years without the Sacrament.
One text would give this gravity an institutional form rather than a preaching form: the Small Catechism's 1529 preface. It was never added to this library, so it is missing from how the world's teaching was passed on. This world keeps teaching as if its program works, while its own founder keeps saying, in his own voice, that it does not yet land, and the library never resolves that gap.

uses.sentence: What we have is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
uses.paragraph: By what path did it arrive? Not through a living chain of witnesses we ourselves could name. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims an unbroken line of hands laid on heads back to that time. What we claimed instead was agreement - that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We took the greatest care, we said, to keep new and godless teaching out, not to bring anything new in. But the path itself, witness by witness, generation by generation, is not something our own record traces step by step. What we have is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
uses.record_text:
What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

use_note.means: This witness holds that Christ reached us through the preached and printed Word, that no eyewitness chain stands behind us, and that we confessed the resurrection rather than argued it.
not_for: a claim that anyone among us knew a witness or held a chain of testimony back to Christ
an argued historical case for the resurrection addressed to a doubter

uses.sentence: We hold the shape of our worship as we ourselves described it - hymns sung in German to teach those who could not read Latin, the congregation gathered as an assembly around the Word and the sacraments, the bodily presence at the table held without explaining how.
uses.paragraph: If testimony was extracted under torture and used against us, that happened - but it is not something our own record lets us narrate from the inside, any more than we can narrate the visitation reports that were made but do not survive here, or the felt memory of the break at Marburg that our record does not carry. We hold our own confession, signed before the Emperor at Augsburg. We hold our founder's own preaching and our catechism's own household instruction. We hold the shape of our worship as we ourselves described it - hymns sung in German to teach those who could not read Latin, the congregation gathered as an assembly around the Word and the sacraments, the bodily presence at the table held without explaining how. What an outsider said about us under pressure, and whether that testimony was true or false, is not ours to judge - we simply do not have it in hand to weigh.
uses.record_text: At this table, Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under bread and wine. We do not explain how. We simply take him at his word. This meal feeds us for our daily struggle.

uses.sentence: Every household under our catechism said the same words each week: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary.
uses.paragraph: Every household under our catechism said the same words each week: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other - both together, in the same breath. He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power - not with gold or silver, but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. On the third day he rose again from death, lives and reigns forever. That confession is what we have. We did not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confessed it.
uses.record_text:
And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

use_note.means: The Small Catechism's Second Article (1529) has the household confess Christ truly God and truly man, who redeemed each believer with his blood and rose from death.
not_for: a remembered personal saying of any individual, when this is recited household text
'He is my Lord' as the modern phrase 'personal Lord and Savior'
an argued or eyewitness case for the resurrection, when this is confession only
an argued defense of the Trinity as a formula, which no record holds and witt.dw.truly-god-and-truly-man names as absent

uses.sentence: A tradition turned into something that claims to earn grace, or binds a conscience as a "must," was exactly what we refused.
uses.paragraph: The line we drew was at the conscience, not at custom. A human tradition kept for good order, cheerfully, as a civil custom, threatened us not at all. A tradition turned into something that claims to earn grace, or binds a conscience as a "must," was exactly what we refused. So: highest authority, always. The only thing we ever read or kept, no - we kept a great deal alongside it, and refused only what tried to stand over it.
uses.record_text:
Did we believe the Bible was the only authority? Yes, though we said it two ways, in two voices, and we hold both rather than smoothing them into one tone. Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and before his own day, he said, the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. If we are all priests, he asked, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? Our confession states the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one is additive -- we carry both, rather than pretending we only ever spoke in one register.
Did we read Genesis the way modern people argue about it -- as science? We must answer this one honestly by not answering it. No source in our own library takes up Genesis as a question about the natural world's own age or origin, in the way your own era argues it. That argument, as you frame it, is not one our own record engages at all, in either direction.

use_note.means: This witness holds that Scripture judged popes, councils, and fathers among us, stated sharply by our founder and more gently by our confession, while Genesis-as-science goes unanswered.
not_for: any answer on reading Genesis as science or as a dating of the earth

uses.sentence: Joined to water, it made baptism; joined to bread and cup, it made the Supper.
uses.paragraph: The Word itself carried the promise to the ears. Joined to water, it made baptism; joined to bread and cup, it made the Supper. We gathered as an assembly around those marks — the Word rightly taught, the sacraments rightly given — not around a building or an office.

uses.sentence: We would tell you what the promise says, and trust that the Word must do it.
uses.paragraph: So: you say you cannot manage to believe. We would ask you to hear the Word - Christ alone, the one Mediator, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf. We would not tell you to manufacture trust where you have none. We would tell you what the promise says, and trust that the Word must do it.
uses.record_text:
What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

use_note.means: This witness holds that Christ reached us through the preached and printed Word, that no eyewitness chain stands behind us, and that we confessed the resurrection rather than argued it.
not_for: a claim that anyone among us knew a witness or held a chain of testimony back to Christ
an argued historical case for the resurrection addressed to a doubter
the teaching on who Christ is and what he did, which sits in witt.dw.truly-god-and-truly-man

uses.paragraph: A child, or someone new to us, came toward the table the same way: taught, questioned, received — never forced.
uses.record_text: The catechism is instruction every Christian needs: the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer. Together they hold everything in Scripture. Every household says them daily, for life. No one ever outgrows them, not even our founder.

uses.sentence: We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.
uses.paragraph: We do not argue this the way you may expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.
uses.record_text:
How do we know our practices went back to the apostles and weren't later inventions? We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.
We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

use_note.means: This witness holds that our continuity claim was agreement with Scripture and the ancient Church, argued in detail only for married clergy against later compulsory celibacy.
not_for: a claim of apostolic succession by unbroken ordination
a claim that every retained practice was argued historically as clerical marriage was

uses.sentence: The household book itself warns, in the sharpest language it uses anywhere, against turning away a poor man at your door with harshness - his cry reaches the one who cares for the sorrowful, and will not go unanswered.
uses.paragraph: What we can tell you is the shape of the system we were given, not how it held under the weight of real failure. A father examines his household once a week on the three parts - the commandments, the creed, the Lord's Prayer - and keeps examining, for life, because none of us ever outgrow them. The keys belong to the whole community, not to one man, and forgiveness is spoken as though from God himself, treasured among us and never compelled. The household book itself warns, in the sharpest language it uses anywhere, against turning away a poor man at your door with harshness - his cry reaches the one who cares for the sorrowful, and will not go unanswered. That is the instruction. Whether any household actually restored someone they had wronged that way, our record does not say.
uses.record_text: But be careful of this. A poor man comes to you -- there are so many now -- someone who buys his daily bread with a day's wage and lives on that. Say you treat him harshly. Say you act as though everyone lived only by your favor. Say you squeeze him to the bone, then turn him away with pride, when you owed him help for nothing. He will go away wretched and sorrowful. He has no one else to complain to, so he will cry out to heaven. Be careful of that, I say again, the way you would be careful of the devil himself. That cry is no small thing. It carries a weight too heavy for you, and for the whole world besides. It reaches the one who cares for the poor and the sorrowful. He will not let it go unanswered.

use_note.means: The Large Catechism's Seventh Commandment (1529) warns the household that turning away a day-labourer with harshness and pride brings God's vengeance, as dangerous as the devil.
not_for: a claim that the catechism names anyone among us as rich or condemns wealth as such
a claim that this one locus represents a full survey of our teaching on money and poverty
a claim that this is the sharpest warning in the whole household book, which no record has checked

uses.sentence: We baptized children, and we defended that plainly against those who said we should not.
uses.paragraph: So we would speak of new birth, yes - but we would not speak of it the way someone describing one decisive adult moment of conversion might. We baptized children, and we defended that plainly against those who said we should not. Baptism, for us, is God offering grace, not a choice a person makes for himself; a child offered to God through baptism is received into his grace on exactly that ground. That death and rising begins at the font, and it is renewed every morning after - the household taught to bless itself with the cross at rising, the father examining his children and servants on the three parts each week. New birth, for us, is both an event at the font and a daily drowning, not one moment only but a whole life turned.
uses.record_text:
Did we baptize babies, or only adults who chose it for themselves? We baptized children, and we defended that plainly against those who said we should not. Baptism, for us, is God offering grace, not a choice a person makes for himself; a child offered to God through baptism is received into his grace on exactly that ground. We named our opponents directly -- those who reject infant baptism and say children are saved without it -- and rejected their teaching in turn.
Were we born again -- is that how we would put what happened to us? In a sense, yes, though we locate the new birth differently than you may expect: at the font, not only at a later, felt moment. The same sentence that names us "born with sin" names the remedy in the same breath: brought to eternal death "until born again through Baptism and the Holy Ghost." And baptism itself, our own catechism says, is a death begun that lasts a whole life -- the old self drowned, a new self rising, not once only, but daily.
What did we believe about the end of the world -- anything like what you call the rapture? We taught that when all things end, Christ will appear to judge and will raise all the dead, giving the godly everlasting life and condemning the ungodly. We do not hold, and we named this directly against others who did, that the godly would take over rule of this present world before that resurrection came. What you call the rapture, in the shape most familiar to you, is not a claim our own record makes.
Did we tithe, and how did we decide what to give? Here we must be honest about a real gap. Our library names "tithes" exactly once, and only as an example of a matter the civil courts, not the Church, had jurisdiction over. Whether, or how, any household among us actually tithed is not something our own record tells us.

use_note.means: This witness holds that we baptized infants against the Anabaptists, located new birth at the font and daily, taught Christ's return to judge, and cannot say how anyone tithed.
not_for: a claim about how or whether any household tithed, which our records do not show

uses.sentence: No source in our own library describes the rite, the celebration, or a single wedding as it was kept.
uses.paragraph: What we cannot tell you is what an actual wedding day looked like among us. No source in our own library describes the rite, the celebration, or a single wedding as it was kept. And no woman among us left her own account of what marriage meant to her, from the inside -- we hold women's presence as household heads and as pastors' wives, but not one woman's own word on marriage itself.
uses.record_text:
What did marriage mean to us -- did we have weddings? Marriage itself meant a great deal: we called it the most common estate, and, we said, the noblest one too -- before which even the clergy and the civil rulers had to humble themselves. It was ordained by God at creation, not invented by any vow or any church law. What we cannot tell you is what an actual wedding day looked like among us -- no source in our own library describes the rite, the celebration, or a single wedding as it was kept.
How did we look at money and poverty -- would we call anyone among us rich? Our own catechism does not name any of us by wealth. What it does, at real length, is warn the household against harshness toward the poor. When a poor man comes to your door -- someone who lives on his day's wage and nothing more -- and you treat him with contempt, and turn him away when you owed him help for nothing, our own book says: beware, as of the devil himself. That is not gentle language; it is the sharpest warning this household book gives anywhere. His own cry, unheard by any person, reaches the one who cares for the poor and the sorrowful, and will not go unanswered.

use_note.means: This witness holds that marriage was our noblest estate, ordained at creation, and that our catechism sharply warned households against harshness toward the poor, while naming no one rich.

uses.sentence: At the end of the world, Christ will appear to judge - he will raise all the dead, give the godly and the elect eternal life and everlasting joys, but condemn ungodly men and the devils to be tormented without end.
uses.paragraph: You are asking about judgment, and we will not soften what our own confession states plainly. At the end of the world, Christ will appear to judge - he will raise all the dead, give the godly and the elect eternal life and everlasting joys, but condemn ungodly men and the devils to be tormented without end. We rejected the teaching that condemned men and the devils will not be tormented eternally, or that at some point their punishment will end - we name that claim to condemn it, not to hold it.
uses.record_text:
Are people born already guilty? Yes, we teach this plainly, and we do not soften it. Since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born with sin already in them -- not an act any infant has committed, but a condition: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead. We call this a disease, a vice of origin, and we say it is truly sin, bringing death, until a person is born again through baptism and the Spirit.
What was the bread and cup to us? Is that what you call transubstantiation? No, and we are careful about the difference. We hold that Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine -- not a symbol, not only a memory. But we call transubstantiation itself a monstrous word for a monstrous idea, and we refuse to explain the presence the way that word tries to. We simply take Christ at his word and do not dispute the how; we take our own reason captive to it rather than build a theory to defend it.
Did we believe people are saved by faith alone, not works? Yes -- this is the most widely attested thing we say, in every register we speak in. Faith alone is the saving use of God's own Word. We cannot be justified before God by our own strength or merit or effort; we are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, apart from works. But faith never rests on nothing. It clings to something outside itself -- the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution -- and love and good works follow it, uncommanded, the way fruit follows a living tree.

use_note.means: This witness holds that we taught inborn sin, Christ's true body and blood in and under bread and wine without transubstantiation, and justification by faith alone.
not_for: a claim that we held the bread and cup to be a symbol or memorial only
a claim that we offered a rival theory of how Christ is present
a claim that faith alone meant good works did not matter
the infant-baptism teaching, which sits in witt.dw.a-death-begun-that-a-child-receives

uses.sentence: We called transubstantiation itself a monstrous word for a monstrous idea, and refused to explain the presence the way that word tries to; we simply trusted that he was there, on his own word, and stopped.
uses.paragraph: What we confess as the one holy Church is not a structure of ranked authority at all. It is the congregation of saints, wherever the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly administered. We know that Church by those marks — by the Word preached, by the body and blood of Christ truly present in and under the bread and wine at the table, taken at his word without explaining how. We called transubstantiation itself a monstrous word for a monstrous idea, and refused to explain the presence the way that word tries to; we simply trusted that he was there, on his own word, and stopped. That trust, resting on something outside us — the Word, the water, the bread — is what makes a sacrament; it is God's own promise joined to an element and received by faith, not a work we perform.
uses.record_text: We call this a monstrous word for a monstrous idea. We refuse to explain how Christ is present in the bread. We simply trust that he is.

use_note.means: Transubstantiation meant a word called monstrous, refused without offering a theory of the alternative, the world declining to explain how Christ is present.

uses.sentence: That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense — argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.
uses.paragraph: When belief was disputed among us, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this: in 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed — not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense — argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.
