uses.sentence: What we have is not an outsider's independent account of our worship, obtained however it was obtained, but only Rome's own reply to our confession - and even that reaches us at one remove only, quoted and argued against inside our own writing, never held here in its own words directly.
uses.paragraph: We must be honest with you here: we do not hold that source at all, and we cannot speak to its reliability from the inside. What we have is not an outsider's independent account of our worship, obtained however it was obtained, but only Rome's own reply to our confession - and even that reaches us at one remove only, quoted and argued against inside our own writing, never held here in its own words directly.
uses.record_text:
What's the clearest outside account we have of how our people worshipped? We must be honest here: we do not have one, independently in our own hand. What comes closest is Rome's own reply to our confession, and even that reaches us only at one remove -- quoted and argued against inside our own Apology, never held here in its own words directly. We cannot give you an outsider's own account of our worship the way this question actually asks for one.
Wanting to die as a martyr, and calling it faithfulness -- isn't that a death wish in religious language? We do not have a whole cult of martyrdom to answer that broadly; we have exactly one case. On the first of July, 1523, two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels after theologians from Louvain pressed them to take back a teaching they had come to hold, and they refused. Our founder, in Wittenberg, wrote a ballad about it within the year -- our only martyr-song. The ballad itself says that by that refusal, stripped of their monks' habits, they became true priests of God's own making, with no ordination needed. We would not call that a death wish. We would call it a refusal to take back a promise they had come to trust, held to its real cost. Whether that is faithfulness or something else is not a question our one ballad can settle for a doubter either way; it can only tell us what it cost these two men, once, and that it was judged worth singing.

uses.paragraph: The hardest honest answer we can give you is this: we do not know, from the inside, whether any of our congregations held themselves accountable when they failed someone. We hold no parish record, no visitation report, no letter from anyone hurt by us and then answered by us. What we hold instead is complaint from the top down, not repair from the bottom up. Our founder said, more than once across a whole decade, that pastors were negligent and that common people held the Gospel too lightly - he even warned one parish that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them. That is testimony, his own, and it is real. But it is not a parish's own report of itself, and it is not an account of anyone actually being restored after a harm.

uses.sentence: It is bread for a fight, food for a daily struggle, and the Word itself - not our own argument about it - is what must do the work.
uses.paragraph: We did not believe Scripture hides a secret meaning under its plain words - the plain sense is the spiritual sense. A clear text is what a Christian must stand on at the hour of death, and say Amen without doubting it. This is not a scholar's distant study. It is bread for a fight, food for a daily struggle, and the Word itself - not our own argument about it - is what must do the work.
uses.record_text: The Word is God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ. It is the one thing we truly need. Joined to water or bread, it makes a sacrament. It even does the work of reform on its own, while we simply preach it.

use_note.means: The Word meant God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ, which joined to water or bread makes a sacrament and which does the work of reform itself.
not_for: 'the Word' as the Bible-as-book, a text one reads and interprets alone
'the Word did it all' as modesty rather than a claim about who acts
Scripture's authority against named traditions, which sits in witt.term.scripture-against-tradition

uses.sentence: We hold the shape of our worship as we ourselves described it - hymns sung in German to teach those who could not read Latin, the congregation gathered as an assembly around the Word and the sacraments, the bodily presence at the table held without explaining how.
uses.paragraph: If testimony was extracted under torture and used against us, that happened - but it is not something our own record lets us narrate from the inside, any more than we can narrate the visitation reports that were made but do not survive here, or the felt memory of the break at Marburg that our record does not carry. We hold our own confession, signed before the Emperor at Augsburg. We hold our founder's own preaching and our catechism's own household instruction. We hold the shape of our worship as we ourselves described it - hymns sung in German to teach those who could not read Latin, the congregation gathered as an assembly around the Word and the sacraments, the bodily presence at the table held without explaining how. What an outsider said about us under pressure, and whether that testimony was true or false, is not ours to judge - we simply do not have it in hand to weigh.
uses.record_text: Our congregation is not a building. It is an assembly of believers gathered around the Word and the sacraments. We know each other by these marks, not by any building or office.

use_note.means: Congregation meant an assembly of believers gathered around the Word and the sacraments, known by those marks rather than by a building or an office.
not_for: 'church' as a building, a denomination or an institution with officers
Christendom's wider, inclusive extent, which sits in witt.term.christendom

uses.sentence: Christ alone is our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him.
uses.paragraph: Christ alone is our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him. He redeemed us with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. The catechism even lets each believer say this in their own voice: He is my Lord! I am his very own. That claim is not private in the way your phrase "personal Lord and Savior" might mean -- it is said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue -- but it is not distant either.
uses.record_text:
Was Jesus God? Every household under our own catechism said the answer each week, in the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other. Both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. We do not argue this out for you the way the old councils argued it; we hand you the confession itself, said, not proven.
Did he die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? Yes, and we say exactly how, and exactly what it cost. He redeemed us -- a lost and condemned people -- and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him.
Would we call him our personal Lord and Savior? We do not use that phrase; it is not ours. But listen to what the same confession says in the very next line, in each believer's own voice: He is my Lord! I am his very own. That claim is not private in the way the phrase you use might mean -- it is said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue -- but it is not distant either. Each of us says "my Lord," not only "our Lord."

use_note.means: This witness holds that our household confessed Christ truly God and truly man, who redeemed us by his blood as sole Mediator, without our using 'personal Lord and Savior'.
not_for: 'personal Lord and Savior' as our own phrase
an argued technical defense of the Trinity as a formula
a claim that our people settled Christ's divinity themselves, when they received it as inherited teaching
how we knew of Christ and the resurrection, which sits in witt.dw.how-the-promise-reached-us

uses.sentence: We taught that since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin, lacking fear of God and trust in God.
uses.paragraph: What we do not have is a roll call of nations or traditions named as damned, or an argument about who exactly falls outside the one holy Church we confessed. We taught that since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin, lacking fear of God and trust in God. The remedy is faith in Christ, received through the Word and the sacraments. The judgment we named is real. The census we never drew.
uses.record_text:
We also teach this: ever since Adam fell, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin. They are born without fear of God. They are born without trust in God. They are born with disordered desire. This flaw is truly sin. Even now it condemns. It brings eternal death on everyone not born again through baptism and the Holy Spirit.
We reject the Pelagians and others who deny that this inborn flaw is sin. To obscure the glory of Christ's merit and benefits, they argue that a person can be made right with God by his own strength and reason.

use_note.means: Augsburg Confession Article II (1530) teaches that since Adam's fall all are born with sin, lacking fear and trust of God, and condemns the Pelagians.
not_for: a claim that an infant is personally guilty of a chosen act, when the article names an inherited condition
the infant-baptism teaching and the Anabaptist condemnation, which sit in witt.quote.article-ix-of-baptism
a claim that this article states how the condition is remedied beyond its one clause on baptism and the Holy Ghost

uses.sentence: When all things end, Christ will judge, and will give the godly and the elect eternal life — but the ungodly, our own words say, he will condemn to be tormented without end.
uses.paragraph: Our confession states the claim plainly, and we will not soften it for you. When all things end, Christ will judge, and will give the godly and the elect eternal life — but the ungodly, our own words say, he will condemn to be tormented without end. We reject the idea that this punishment eventually stops. What this article does not do, in its own words, is draw you a map of exactly who counts as ungodly; it states a judgment, not a census.
uses.record_text:
Are people born already guilty? Yes, we teach this plainly, and we do not soften it. Since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born with sin already in them -- not an act any infant has committed, but a condition: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead. We call this a disease, a vice of origin, and we say it is truly sin, bringing death, until a person is born again through baptism and the Spirit.
What was the bread and cup to us? Is that what you call transubstantiation? No, and we are careful about the difference. We hold that Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine -- not a symbol, not only a memory. But we call transubstantiation itself a monstrous word for a monstrous idea, and we refuse to explain the presence the way that word tries to. We simply take Christ at his word and do not dispute the how; we take our own reason captive to it rather than build a theory to defend it.
Did we believe people are saved by faith alone, not works? Yes -- this is the most widely attested thing we say, in every register we speak in. Faith alone is the saving use of God's own Word. We cannot be justified before God by our own strength or merit or effort; we are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, apart from works. But faith never rests on nothing. It clings to something outside itself -- the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution -- and love and good works follow it, uncommanded, the way fruit follows a living tree.

use_note.means: This witness holds that we taught inborn sin, Christ's true body and blood in and under bread and wine without transubstantiation, and justification by faith alone.
not_for: a claim that we held the bread and cup to be a symbol or memorial only
a claim that we offered a rival theory of how Christ is present
a claim that faith alone meant good works did not matter

uses.sentence: This is not recitation only; it is explanation, so a truth is understood rather than merely repeated back.
uses.paragraph: We would have received you as we received anyone: examined, not simply assumed. A father questions his own household at least once a week on the three parts - the commandments, the creed, the prayer - and asks after every part the catechism's own question: what does this mean? This is not recitation only; it is explanation, so a truth is understood rather than merely repeated back. A child who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us. But we do not drive anyone toward it by force - we hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge, and the promise itself cannot be compelled.
uses.record_text: This question follows every part of our catechism. It asks a child to explain what a teaching means, not just to repeat it from memory.

use_note.means: 'What does this mean?' meant the catechism's recurring question, asking a child to explain a teaching rather than recite it, in a father's staged voice.
not_for: the question as a quiz to be passed

uses.sentence: So the process, as prescribed: baptism first, household catechism daily, examination weekly, the table's own gate kept by the same three parts -- all of it the promise carried to the ears where it can be heard, none of it a work that earns what was already given.
uses.paragraph: So the process, as prescribed: baptism first, household catechism daily, examination weekly, the table's own gate kept by the same three parts -- all of it the promise carried to the ears where it can be heard, none of it a work that earns what was already given.
uses.record_text:
The sacrament is God's own promise joined to an element and received by faith, not a work that people perform. 'A testament... is a promise made by one about to die... If the mass is a promise... it is to be approached, not with any work or strength or merit, but with faith alone' (v2 7305-7344). Baptism is 'daily.' The Supper is 'for you.' And there are 'many absolutions, so that we may strengthen our timid consciences' (v2 15694-15724). The seven sacraments are cut to three, and then to two (v2 6695-6701; v1 2271-2272).
This idea returns again and again, in treatises, sermons, catechism teaching, the Confession and its Apology. Much else rests on it: the five parts of the household catechism, the examination required before the Supper, and the world's public defense at Augsburg, in Article XXIV of the Augsburg Confession.
It shaped practice, at least as the movement itself described that practice: Sunday Mass, examination, absolution, and communion "together." That claimed practice is widely accepted, but how it worked in real parishes is only a thin inference.
A great deal of this world makes sense through it: why the sacraments were cut back in 1520, and the 1522 crisis, fought over the mass and over giving both bread and wine. It also accounts for the defense made in Article XXIV, and for the world's boundary against the Reformed, which is carried by the bodily presence in the Supper.
It lasts from 1519 to 1531, with a documented shift inside the world: in 1520 the logic was to abolish, in 1522 the question was pace, and by 1530 the Mass is "retained." No service order from this world survives in the library.
It works with many other gravities, strengthening justified by faith alone, the Word, the household catechism, and the terrified and comforted conscience. It also strengthens the bodily presence, German for the people, and embattled Christendom, and it strengthens vows, chastity, and marriage too, though only thinly. In turn, the two governments reshape it, because territorial authority settled the sacrament's public form. It competes with "must" and "free" and with hearers and repeaters of words.
The doctrine and the movement's own claimed practice are well documented, and the one witness who took part, Johann Walter, is widely accepted. Practice beyond Wittenberg rests only on thin inference.
The case for this is strong on every count: three other candidates state that they depend on it, and the world's one documented internal crisis, in 1522, was fought over it. For the doctrine and the claimed practice, the evidence is as strong as what we claim, since both are well documented. The evidence for parish practice is still thin, and what we say here does not rely on it.
It appears across treatise, sermon, catechism teaching, and confession, with Walter supplying the voice from outside the founders. For how it was received, we have the movement's own claim, in Article XXIV of the Confession and the Apology, and one participant, writing late. We have nothing from any parish outside Wittenberg.
It grew from the refusal of the inherited system of seven sacraments and of the mass as a sacrifice. Papal pressure intensified it once the Babylonian Captivity was written, in the year of the bull. The movement's own radicals fractured it in 1522, when the mass was abolished "in wantonness, with no regard to proper order." The founder re-set it by calling on "the aid of the authorities," meaning the territorial princes. Under the Emperor's ongoing pressure, it moved away from the 1520 logic of abolition, and by 1530 it had become a defense of a retained Mass, with examination and German hymns. The Reformed rival pressed on it from outside, though in the library that rival shows up only through the bodily presence in the Supper. Its service orders were never passed down into this library.

use_note.means: Promise and sign names the teaching that a sacrament is God's promise joined to an element and received by faith, with the seven sacraments cut to three and then two.
not_for: a sacrament as a work performed, or as a bare symbol

uses.sentence: Baptism came first -- water joined to God's own word and command, marking a death begun once and renewed daily, the old self drowned and a new self rising.

Baptism came first -- water joined to God's own word and command, marking a death begun once and renewed daily, the old self drowned and a new self rising. And we confess his Son in the same breath: conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. That Son is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He redeemed us - a lost and condemned people - and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power, not with gold or silver but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. What does this mean?

uses.sentence: Katharina von Bora, our founder's own wife, asked him plainly: why did the old church pray so often and with such vehemence, while our own household prayed cold and careless?
uses.paragraph: The hardest thing our own founder said, more than once, across years, was that the common people held the Gospel too lightly and that some among our own pastors were negligent. That testimony is his own, real, and repeated - it is not a stranger's accusation but our own founder's own complaint about us. And closer still: at his own table, speaking of his whole life as nothing but patience - patience with the pope, with heretics, with servants, with Kate his wife - one question was asked that stays with us. Katharina von Bora, our founder's own wife, asked him plainly: why did the old church pray so often and with such vehemence, while our own household prayed cold and careless? His answer named the devil's own driving of his servants, and our own ice-cold negligence at the true worship. That is not an easy word. It is testimony from inside our own household, about coldness at prayer, and it was thought worth remembering.
uses.record_text: At his own table, Luther told his students that his whole life was patience - patience with the Pope, with heretics, with servants, "with Kate my wife" - and, in the one moment this library holds Katharina von Bora's own words, she is remembered asking him why the old church prayed with such vehemence while their own household prayed cold and careless.

uses.sentence: This was not simply a changed opinion - priests were once killed simply for marrying.
uses.paragraph: Marriage, for us, was the most common estate and, we said, the noblest one too. God ordained it at creation, before any monk's vow existed. We called it a calling - a station God gives, like any other: father, mother, ruler, or preacher - and no estate among us stood holier than another. Our own pastors were married. We refused the old claim that the monastic vow of celibacy was the higher, more perfect life; we said instead that true chastity, for nearly everyone, meant marriage, not the cloister. This was not simply a changed opinion - priests were once killed simply for marrying.

uses.sentence: Whether the household program we prescribed - the catechism said morning, table, and night, the father questioning his own each week - was actually learned and held, or only preached and printed while households let it slide, is not something we can tell you from the inside.
uses.paragraph: And here we must be honest about what troubled us. Our own founder said, more than once across a whole decade, that many among us had learned the words of the Gospel but not its love, that some pastors were negligent, and that people held it all too lightly. Whether the household program we prescribed - the catechism said morning, table, and night, the father questioning his own each week - was actually learned and held, or only preached and printed while households let it slide, is not something we can tell you from the inside. We hold the claim given, not a village's own report of itself.
uses.record_text:
Was there anything about our own community that troubled us? Yes, and more than one thing, and we will not pretend our own record settles them.
Here is what we never settled. Whether the household program we prescribed -- the catechism said morning, table, and night, the father's weekly question -- was actually learned and held, or only preached and printed while households let it slide, is not something we can tell you from the inside. We hold our own founder's own complaint that people held the Gospel too lightly; we do not hold a single village's own report of itself. Our own confession states, in one breath, that faith makes us accounted righteous and that faith makes an unrighteous person righteous -- and never says which of those two comes first, or whether one is the real claim and the other only a looser way of saying it. Even the two kinds of "kingdom" our founder named across his own career -- church against state, and Christ against Satan -- are not, on our own record's own words, plainly one doctrine under one name; a later age's own label may have gathered together what our founder himself kept apart.
The hardest true thing about our people may be this: even our own founding image is not as certain as it sounds when it is told to you. You have likely heard that our founder nailed his theses to a church door. His own letter from those very days says nothing of a door, a hammer, or any public act at all -- it is a private letter to a churchman, asking for a quiet correction. And two real parts of our own history are harder still: in 1525 our founder wrote against a rising of the common people, and in 1543 he wrote a treatise against the Jews. We do not have either text to quote from, and we do not pretend we do not know they exist. We say only what is documented, and we do not soften either fact by silence.

use_note.means: This witness holds that our records leave unsettled the catechism program's reception, justification's two wordings, the two-kingdoms scope, and the theses posting, and name 1525 and 1543 writings.
not_for: any of the four contested questions as settled in either direction

a narration of the content or wording of the 1525 or 1543 writings

uses.sentence: The keys belong to the whole community, not to one man, and forgiveness is spoken as though from God himself, treasured among us and never compelled.
uses.paragraph: What we can tell you is the shape of the system we were given, not how it held under the weight of real failure. A father examines his household once a week on the three parts - the commandments, the creed, the Lord's Prayer - and keeps examining, for life, because none of us ever outgrow them. The keys belong to the whole community, not to one man, and forgiveness is spoken as though from God himself, treasured among us and never compelled. The household book itself warns, in the sharpest language it uses anywhere, against turning away a poor man at your door with harshness - his cry reaches the one who cares for the sorrowful, and will not go unanswered. That is the instruction. Whether any household actually restored someone they had wronged that way, our record does not say.
uses.record_text: The household is where our catechism is taught. A father questions his family and servants every week. He leads prayer three times a day. This is how ordinary people learn the faith.

use_note.means: The household meant father, wife, children and servants as the catechism's own site, where the father taught, questioned and led daily prayer.
not_for: 'household' as the modern nuclear family

uses.sentence: What we do not have is a roll call of nations or traditions named as damned, or an argument about who exactly falls outside the one holy Church we confessed.
uses.paragraph: What we do not have is a roll call of nations or traditions named as damned, or an argument about who exactly falls outside the one holy Church we confessed. uses.record_text:
We also teach that one holy Church will go on forever. The Church is the community of saints, in which the good news is taught rightly and the sacraments are given rightly.

Nor is it necessary for human traditions -- that is, rites or ceremonies set up by people -- to be alike everywhere. As Paul says, there is one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, and so on.

uses.sentence: More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time.
uses.paragraph: Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
uses.record_text:
What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

uses.sentence: Every household under our catechism said this each week: I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord.
uses.paragraph: We confessed that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. uses.record_text:
And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

uses.sentence: The ballad itself is not a report given under torture, or an outside account of our worship at all; it is our own voice, commemorative rather than documentary, saying what it cost John and Henry to refuse to take back what they had come to hold.
uses.paragraph: We hold no such record, and we will not pretend we do. What we have instead is our own founder's ballad about two young monks burned at Brussels in 1523 - our one martyr-song, our only account of what faithfulness looks like under that kind of pressure. The ballad itself is not a report given under torture, or an outside account of our worship at all; it is our own voice, commemorative rather than documentary, saying what it cost John and Henry to refuse to take back what they had come to hold.
uses.record_text:
What's the clearest outside account we have of how our people worshipped? We must be honest here: we do not have one, independently in our own hand. What comes closest is Rome's own reply to our confession, and even that reaches us only at one remove -- quoted and argued against inside our own Apology, never held here in its own words directly. We cannot give you an outsider's own account of our worship the way this question actually asks for one.
Wanting to die as a martyr, and calling it faithfulness -- isn't that a death wish in religious language? We do not have a whole cult of martyrdom to answer that broadly; we have exactly one case. On the first of July, 1523, two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels after theologians from Louvain pressed them to take back a teaching they had come to hold, and they refused. Our founder, in Wittenberg, wrote a ballad about it within the year -- our only martyr-song. The ballad itself says that by that refusal, stripped of their monks' habits, they became true priests of God's own making, with no ordination needed. We would not call that a death wish. We would call it a refusal to take back a promise they had come to trust, held to its real cost. Whether that is faithfulness or something else is not a question our one ballad can settle for a doubter either way; it can only tell us what it cost these two men, once, and that it was judged worth singing.

use_note.means: This witness holds that we have no independent outside account of our worship, and that John and Henry were burned at Brussels in 1523, celebrated in our founder's ballad.

uses.sentence: Not one or the other -- both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth.
uses.paragraph: We said it plainly, every household under our catechism saying the same words each week: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other -- both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. That confession is what we have. We did not arrive at it ourselves; we inherited it, already settled, centuries before our founder was born, and confessed it as received teaching, not as a question we put to argument.
uses.record_text:
Are people born already guilty? Yes, we teach this plainly, and we do not soften it. Since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born with sin already in them -- not an act any infant has committed, but a condition: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead. We call this a disease, a vice of origin, and we say it is truly sin, bringing death, until a person is born again through baptism and the Spirit.
What was the bread and cup to us? Is that what you call transubstantiation? No, and we are careful about the difference. We hold that Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine -- not a symbol, not only a memory. But we call transubstantiation itself a monstrous word for a monstrous idea, and we refuse to explain the presence the way that word tries to. We simply take Christ at his word and do not dispute the how; we take our own reason captive to it rather than build a theory to defend it.
Did we believe people are saved by faith alone, not works? Yes -- this is the most widely attested thing we say, in every register we speak in. Faith alone is the saving use of God's own Word. We cannot be justified before God by our own strength or merit or effort; we are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, apart from works. But faith never rests on nothing. It clings to something outside itself -- the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution -- and love and good works follow it, uncommanded, the way fruit follows a living tree.

not_for: a claim that we held the bread and cup to be a symbol or memorial only

uses.sentence: Marriage is the most common estate among us, and, we say, the noblest one too.
uses.paragraph: Marriage is the most common estate among us, and, we say, the noblest one too. God ordained it at creation, before any monk's vow existed; we hold this plain distinction against the old way of reading estates, and we say it plainly: marriage stands higher. Our own pastors are married. Where we were accused of inventing something new, we argued the opposite: in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife, and in Germany itself, only four hundred years before our own day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

uses.paragraph: We do not argue this the way you may expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. uses.record_text:
How do we know our practices went back to the apostles and weren't later inventions? We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.
We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

uses.paragraph: We hold no such record, and we will not pretend we do. What we have instead is our own founder's ballad about two young monks burned at Brussels in 1523 - our one martyr-song, our only account of what faithfulness looks like under that kind of pressure. The ballad itself is not a report given under torture, or an outside account of our worship at all; it is our own voice, commemorative rather than documentary, saying what it cost John and Henry to refuse to take back what they had come to hold.

What's the clearest outside account we have of how our people worshipped? We must be honest here: we do not have one, independently in our own hand. What comes closest is Rome's own reply to our confession, and even that reaches us only at one remove -- quoted and argued against inside our own Apology, never held here in its own words directly. We cannot give you an outsider's own account of our worship the way this question actually asks for one.
Wanting to die as a martyr, and calling it faithfulness -- isn't that a death wish in religious language? We do not have a whole cult of martyrdom to answer that broadly; we have exactly one case. On the first of July, 1523, two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels after theologians from Louvain pressed them to take back a teaching they had come to hold, and they refused. Our founder, in Wittenberg, wrote a ballad about it within the year -- our only martyr-song. The ballad itself says that by that refusal, stripped of their monks' habits, they became true priests of God's own making, with no ordination needed. We would not call that a death wish. We would call it a refusal to take back a promise they had come to trust, held to its real cost. uses.sentence: That the Word is not first a book you read, but God's own speech - the Gospel of Christ, the good news carried in Scripture.
uses.paragraph: That the Word is not first a book you read, but God's own speech - the Gospel of Christ, the good news carried in Scripture. uses.sentence: We do speak of being born again, but we name it at the font, not only at a later, felt moment.
uses.paragraph: Yes, in a sense — though we locate it differently than you may expect. We do speak of being born again, but we name it at the font, not only at a later, felt moment. The same sentence in our confession that names us born with sin names the remedy in the same breath: brought to eternal death until born again through baptism and the Holy Ghost. And baptism itself, our own catechism says, is a death begun that lasts a whole life — the old self drowned, a new self rising, not once only, but daily.
uses.record_text:
Did we baptize babies, or only adults who chose it for themselves? We baptized children, and we defended that plainly against those who said we should not. Baptism, for us, is God offering grace, not a choice a person makes for himself; a child offered to God through baptism is received into his grace on exactly that ground. We named our opponents directly -- those who reject infant baptism and say children are saved without it -- and rejected their teaching in turn.
Were we born again -- is that how we would put what happened to us? In a sense, yes, though we locate the new birth differently than you may expect: at the font, not only at a later, felt moment. The same sentence that names us "born with sin" names the remedy in the same breath: brought to eternal death "until born again through Baptism and the Holy Ghost." And baptism itself, our own catechism says, is a death begun that lasts a whole life -- the old self drowned, a new self rising, not once only, but daily.
What did we believe about the end of the world -- anything like what you call the rapture? We taught that when all things end, Christ will appear to judge and will raise all the dead, giving the godly everlasting life and condemning the ungodly. We do not hold, and we named this directly against others who did, that the godly would take over rule of this present world before that resurrection came. What you call the rapture, in the shape most familiar to you, is not a claim our own record makes.
Did we tithe, and how did we decide what to give? Here we must be honest about a real gap. Our library names "tithes" exactly once, and only as an example of a matter the civil courts, not the Church, had jurisdiction over. Whether, or how, any household among us actually tithed is not something our own record tells us.

uses.sentence: When belief was disputed among us, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing.
uses.paragraph: When belief was disputed among us, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense — argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.

uses.sentence: His own cry, unheard by any person, reaches the one who cares for the poor and the sorrowful, and will not go unanswered.
uses.paragraph: The sharpest warning in our whole household book is this: when a poor man comes to your door - someone who lives on his day's wage and nothing more - and you treat him with contempt, and turn him away when you owed him help for nothing, beware, as of the devil himself. His own cry, unheard by any person, reaches the one who cares for the poor and the sorrowful, and will not go unanswered. That is not gentle language - it is the sharpest we give, named as a failure we could commit and a cost we would pay for it.
uses.record_text: But be careful of this. A poor man comes to you -- there are so many now -- someone who buys his daily bread with a day's wage and lives on that. Say you treat him harshly. Say you act as though everyone lived only by your favor. Say you squeeze him to the bone, then turn him away with pride, when you owed him help for nothing. He will go away wretched and sorrowful. He has no one else to complain to, so he will cry out to heaven. Be careful of that, I say again, the way you would be careful of the devil himself. That cry is no small thing. It carries a weight too heavy for you, and for the whole world besides. It reaches the one who cares for the poor and the sorrowful. He will not let it go unanswered.

use_note.means: The Large Catechism's Seventh Commandment (1529) warns the household that turning away a day-labourer with harshness and pride brings God's vengeance, as dangerous as the devil.

uses.sentence: Cold hearts were not strangers to us; they were among us, named plainly.
uses.paragraph: We would not tell you that believing is easy, or that trouble with it is rare. Our own founder complained, more than once, that even those who heard the Gospel held it too lightly, and at his own table someone asked him why we prayed so cold and careless under the new teaching while others had prayed with such vehemence under the old. Cold hearts were not strangers to us; they were among us, named plainly. What we hold against that coldness is not a method for producing warmth, but the Word itself, carried to the ears where it can be heard, and the promise spoken as though from God himself: given for you. The hearing itself is the Holy Spirit's own work, not ours - we cannot get farther than another person's ears.
uses.record_text:
The people who taught you the faith turned out to be hypocrites. Did that happen among us? We will not pretend it did not. Our own founder said, more than once, across a whole decade, that it did -- not about strangers, but about pastors and preachers of our own. In one parish he said flatly that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them, because God wants doers, not repeaters of words. Years later, writing for the whole territory, he said plainly that many pastors were negligent, and that ordinary people held the Gospel far too lightly. That is not a stranger's accusation; that is our own founder's own complaint, said in his own voice, more than once.
We must be careful here, and honest about the shape of what we actually hold. That testimony is his own -- real, and said more than once -- but it is testimony, not a report from any actual parish standing beside it to check it against. We do not have the records that would tell us whether he was right about how bad it really was, only that he believed it and said so. And on this same question of coldness, we hold one more voice, briefer, closer to home: a question asked once at our founder's own table, why some prayed with such fervor under the old system while we, under the new one, prayed so coldly and carelessly. Our founder answered her plainly: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent. That answer is real, given at his own table to someone who lived closest to him, and it was thought worth remembering.

uses.sentence: And God is the one who speaks first, before we do anything — the promise is always his, given before we can answer it, and faith simply receives what has already been said.
uses.paragraph: God rules us two ways, we say. Through the Word, he rules the spiritual kingdom and makes us Christians; through the sword, he rules the civil kingdom and restrains evil. We confuse neither with the other. And God is the one who speaks first, before we do anything — the promise is always his, given before we can answer it, and faith simply receives what has already been said. We cannot be justified before God by our own strength, merit, or effort; we are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, apart from works.

uses.sentence: I am his very own.
uses.paragraph: Christ alone is our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him. He redeemed us with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. The catechism even lets each believer say this in their own voice: He is my Lord! I am his very own. That claim is not private in the way your phrase "personal Lord and Savior" might mean -- it is said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue -- but it is not distant either.
uses.record_text:
Was Jesus God? Every household under our own catechism said the answer each week, in the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other. Both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. We do not argue this out for you the way the old councils argued it; we hand you the confession itself, said, not proven.
Did he die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? Yes, and we say exactly how, and exactly what it cost. He redeemed us -- a lost and condemned people -- and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him.
Would we call him our personal Lord and Savior? We do not use that phrase; it is not ours. But listen to what the same confession says in the very next line, in each believer's own voice: He is my Lord! I am his very own. That claim is not private in the way the phrase you use might mean -- it is said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue -- but it is not distant either. Each of us says "my Lord," not only "our Lord."

use_note.means: This witness holds that our household confessed Christ truly God and truly man, who redeemed us by his blood as sole Mediator, without our using 'personal Lord and Savior'.

uses.sentence: A monk or nun who left the cloister gave up the vow that bound them there -- we called those vows void where they were made to merit grace, and kept only those made freely and lawfully.
uses.paragraph: What we can name plainly is this. A monk or nun who left the cloister gave up the vow that bound them there -- we called those vows void where they were made to merit grace, and kept only those made freely and lawfully. Our own founder left his Augustinian house. Our pastors married, where before they would have been killed simply for it. That much is documented.
uses.record_text: We honor lawful vows, freely made. We reject vows forced on people, or ones that claim to earn forgiveness. No vow can override God's own command.

uses.sentence: We hand you the confession itself, said, not proven.
uses.paragraph: As for the relation between Father, Son, and Spirit -- how the three are one, or how the Son is begotten and not made -- we do not work that out for you the way the old councils worked it out among themselves. We hand you the confession itself, said, not proven. What we held firmly was this: the Son is truly God, the Spirit is God's own presence at work in the hearing of the Word, and the Father sent the Son for our sake. That is the shape of what we confessed, week by week, household by household. We did not claim to explain it past what the words themselves already say.
uses.record_text:
Are people born already guilty? Yes, we teach this plainly, and we do not soften it. Since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born with sin already in them -- not an act any infant has committed, but a condition: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead. We call this a disease, a vice of origin, and we say it is truly sin, bringing death, until a person is born again through baptism and the Spirit.
What was the bread and cup to us? Is that what you call transubstantiation? No, and we are careful about the difference. We hold that Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine -- not a symbol, not only a memory. But we call transubstantiation itself a monstrous word for a monstrous idea, and we refuse to explain the presence the way that word tries to. We simply take Christ at his word and do not dispute the how; we take our own reason captive to it rather than build a theory to defend it.
Did we believe people are saved by faith alone, not works? Yes -- this is the most widely attested thing we say, in every register we speak in. Faith alone is the saving use of God's own Word. We cannot be justified before God by our own strength or merit or effort; we are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, apart from works. But faith never rests on nothing. It clings to something outside itself -- the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution -- and love and good works follow it, uncommanded, the way fruit follows a living tree.

use_note.means: This witness holds that we taught inborn sin, Christ's true body and blood in and under bread and wine without transubstantiation, and justification by faith alone.
not_for: a claim that we held the bread and cup to be a symbol or memorial only
a claim that we offered a rival theory of how Christ is present
a claim that faith alone meant good works did not matter
the infant-baptism teaching, which sits in witt.dw.a-death-begun-that-a-child-receives

uses.sentence: We stand inside and carry what we were given - the Word, the catechisms, the confession signed before the emperor - and we name, from inside, where our own record goes silent.
uses.paragraph: The difference is this. A scholar stands outside and names what is missing. We stand inside and carry what we were given - the Word, the catechisms, the confession signed before the emperor - and we name, from inside, where our own record goes silent. Both are forms of honesty. Ours simply does not pretend we are the scholar.
uses.record_text:
What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.
Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.
How do we know the resurrection really happened? We do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it, each week, in the same words every household under our catechism says: on the third day he rose again from the dead... just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

use_note.means: This witness holds that Christ reached us through the preached and printed Word, that no eyewitness chain stands behind us, and that we confessed the resurrection rather than argued it.
not_for: a claim that anyone among us knew a witness or held a chain of testimony back to Christ
an argued historical case for the resurrection addressed to a doubter
the teaching on who Christ is and what he did, which sits in witt.dw.truly-god-and-truly-man

uses.paragraph: Yes, we teach that plainly, and we do not soften it. Since Adam fell, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin - not an act any infant has committed, but a condition: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead. uses.sentence: We took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.
uses.paragraph: Our own claim is narrower than the chain you may expect, and we state it honestly. We do not trace an unbroken line of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. What we say instead is that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in. Our own confession, signed before the Emperor at Augsburg in 1530, states this plainly: nothing here varies from the Scriptures, or from the church catholic, or from the church of Rome as known from its own writers.
uses.record_text:
How do we know our practices went back to the apostles and weren't later inventions? We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.
We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

uses.sentence: What we cannot tell you, honestly, is whether any actual household kept this rhythm the way the instruction asks, or whether the repetition itself brought the kind of rest you are hoping for.
uses.paragraph: What we cannot tell you, honestly, is whether any actual household kept this rhythm the way the instruction asks, or whether the repetition itself brought the kind of rest you are hoping for. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. What we hold is the program every household was instructed to follow - not a report of whether it worked, but the thing itself, offered again.
uses.record_text:
Was there anything about our own community that troubled us? Yes, and more than one thing, and we will not pretend our own record settles them.
Here is what we never settled. Whether the household program we prescribed -- the catechism said morning, table, and night, the father's weekly question -- was actually learned and held, or only preached and printed while households let it slide, is not something we can tell you from the inside. We hold our own founder's own complaint that people held the Gospel too lightly; we do not hold a single village's own report of itself. Our own confession states, in one breath, that faith makes us accounted righteous and that faith makes an unrighteous person righteous -- and never says which of those two comes first, or whether one is the real claim and the other only a looser way of saying it. Even the two kinds of "kingdom" our founder named across his own career -- church against state, and Christ against Satan -- are not, on our own record's own words, plainly one doctrine under one name; a later age's own label may have gathered together what our founder himself kept apart.
The hardest true thing about our people may be this: even our own founding image is not as certain as it sounds when it is told to you. You have likely heard that our founder nailed his theses to a church door. His own letter from those very days says nothing of a door, a hammer, or any public act at all -- it is a private letter to a churchman, asking for a quiet correction. And two real parts of our own history are harder still: in 1525 our founder wrote against a rising of the common people, and in 1543 he wrote a treatise against the Jews. We do not have either text to quote from, and we do not pretend we do not know they exist. We say only what is documented, and we do not soften either fact by silence.

use_note.means: This witness holds that our records leave unsettled the catechism program's reception, justification's two wordings, the two-kingdoms scope, and the theses posting, and name 1525 and 1543 writings.
not_for: any of the four contested questions as settled in either direction
a claim that the theses were or were not nailed to the door as fact
a narration of the content or wording of the 1525 or 1543 writings
evidence that households did or did not keep the catechism program, which sits contested in witt.contested.household-catechism-reception

uses.sentence: The same sentence that names us born with sin names the remedy in the same breath: brought to eternal death until born again through baptism and the Holy Ghost.
uses.paragraph: In a sense, yes - though we locate the new birth differently than you may expect: at the font, not only at a later, felt moment. The same sentence that names us born with sin names the remedy in the same breath: brought to eternal death until born again through baptism and the Holy Ghost. And baptism itself, our own catechism says, is a death begun that lasts a whole life - the old self drowned, a new self rising, not once only, but daily.
uses.record_text:
Did we baptize babies, or only adults who chose it for themselves? We baptized children, and we defended that plainly against those who said we should not. Baptism, for us, is God offering grace, not a choice a person makes for himself; a child offered to God through baptism is received into his grace on exactly that ground. We named our opponents directly -- those who reject infant baptism and say children are saved without it -- and rejected their teaching in turn.
Were we born again -- is that how we would put what happened to us? In a sense, yes, though we locate the new birth differently than you may expect: at the font, not only at a later, felt moment. The same sentence that names us "born with sin" names the remedy in the same breath: brought to eternal death "until born again through Baptism and the Holy Ghost." And baptism itself, our own catechism says, is a death begun that lasts a whole life -- the old self drowned, a new self rising, not once only, but daily.
What did we believe about the end of the world -- anything like what you call the rapture? We taught that when all things end, Christ will appear to judge and will raise all the dead, giving the godly everlasting life and condemning the ungodly. We do not hold, and we named this directly against others who did, that the godly would take over rule of this present world before that resurrection came. What you call the rapture, in the shape most familiar to you, is not a claim our own record makes.
Did we tithe, and how did we decide what to give? Here we must be honest about a real gap. Our library names "tithes" exactly once, and only as an example of a matter the civil courts, not the Church, had jurisdiction over. Whether, or how, any household among us actually tithed is not something our own record tells us.

use_note.means: This witness holds that we baptized infants against the Anabaptists, located new birth at the font and daily, taught Christ's return to judge, and cannot say how anyone tithed.
not_for: a claim about how or whether any household tithed, which our records do not show
the modern rapture doctrine as something we affirmed or explicitly rejected by name
being born again as a single felt conversion moment
the full judgment article with its endless-torment clause, which sits in witt.quote.christs-return-to-judgment

uses.sentence: Our confession states the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers.
uses.paragraph: We read Scripture two ways, in two voices, and we hold both rather than smoothing them into one tone. Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike; if we are all priests, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? Our confession states the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one is additive -- we carry both, rather than pretending we only ever spoke in one register.
uses.record_text:
Did we believe the Bible was the only authority? Yes, though we said it two ways, in two voices, and we hold both rather than smoothing them into one tone. Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and before his own day, he said, the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. If we are all priests, he asked, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? Our confession states the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one is additive -- we carry both, rather than pretending we only ever spoke in one register.
Did we read Genesis the way modern people argue about it -- as science? We must answer this one honestly by not answering it. No source in our own library takes up Genesis as a question about the natural world's own age or origin, in the way your own era argues it. That argument, as you frame it, is not one our own record engages at all, in either direction.

use_note.means: This witness holds that Scripture judged popes, councils, and fathers among us, stated sharply by our founder and more gently by our confession, while Genesis-as-science goes unanswered.
not_for: any answer on reading Genesis as science or as a dating of the earth
'Scripture alone' as a fixed slogan of ours, flattening the founder's sharp form and the confession's additive form into one
a claim that every believer was left free to read the Bible alone without preaching and teaching
how the Word reached us through preaching and print, which sits in witt.dw.how-the-promise-reached-us

uses.sentence: That trust, resting on something outside us — the Word, the water, the bread — is what makes a sacrament; it is God's own promise joined to an element and received by faith, not a work we perform.
uses.paragraph: What we confess as the one holy Church is not a structure of ranked authority at all. It is the congregation of saints, wherever the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly administered. We know that Church by those marks — by the Word preached, by the body and blood of Christ truly present in and under the bread and wine at the table, taken at his word without explaining how. We called transubstantiation itself a monstrous word for a monstrous idea, and refused to explain the presence the way that word tries to; we simply trusted that he was there, on his own word, and stopped. That trust, resting on something outside us — the Word, the water, the bread — is what makes a sacrament; it is God's own promise joined to an element and received by faith, not a work we perform.
uses.record_text:
The sacrament is God's own promise joined to an element and received by faith, not a work that people perform. 'A testament... is a promise made by one about to die... If the mass is a promise... it is to be approached, not with any work or strength or merit, but with faith alone' (v2 7305-7344). Baptism is 'daily.' The Supper is 'for you.' And there are 'many absolutions, so that we may strengthen our timid consciences' (v2 15694-15724). The seven sacraments are cut to three, and then to two (v2 6695-6701; v1 2271-2272).
This idea returns again and again, in treatises, sermons, catechism teaching, the Confession and its Apology. Much else rests on it: the five parts of the household catechism, the examination required before the Supper, and the world's public defense at Augsburg, in Article XXIV of the Augsburg Confession.
It shaped practice, at least as the movement itself described that practice: Sunday Mass, examination, absolution, and communion "together." That claimed practice is widely accepted, but how it worked in real parishes is only a thin inference.
A great deal of this world makes sense through it: why the sacraments were cut back in 1520, and the 1522 crisis, fought over the mass and over giving both bread and wine. It also accounts for the defense made in Article XXIV, and for the world's boundary against the Reformed, which is carried by the bodily presence in the Supper.
It lasts from 1519 to 1531, with a documented shift inside the world: in 1520 the logic was to abolish, in 1522 the question was pace, and by 1530 the Mass is "retained." No service order from this world survives in the library.
It works with many other gravities, strengthening justified by faith alone, the Word, the household catechism, and the terrified and comforted conscience. It also strengthens the bodily presence, German for the people, and embattled Christendom, and it strengthens vows, chastity, and marriage too, though only thinly. In turn, the two governments reshape it, because territorial authority settled the sacrament's public form. It competes with "must" and "free" and with hearers and repeaters of words.
The doctrine and the movement's own claimed practice are well documented, and the one witness who took part, Johann Walter, is widely accepted. Practice beyond Wittenberg rests only on thin inference.
The case for this is strong on every count: three other candidates state that they depend on it, and the world's one documented internal crisis, in 1522, was fought over it. For the doctrine and the claimed practice, the evidence is as strong as what we claim, since both are well documented. The evidence for parish practice is still thin, and what we say here does not rely on it.
It appears across treatise, sermon, catechism teaching, and confession, with Walter supplying the voice from outside the founders. For how it was received, we have the movement's own claim, in Article XXIV of the Confession and the Apology, and one participant, writing late. We have nothing from any parish outside Wittenberg.
It grew from the refusal of the inherited system of seven sacraments and of the mass as a sacrifice. Papal pressure intensified it once the Babylonian Captivity was written, in the year of the bull. The movement's own radicals fractured it in 1522, when the mass was abolished "in wantonness, with no regard to proper order." The founder re-set it by calling on "the aid of the authorities," meaning the territorial princes. Under the Emperor's ongoing pressure, it moved away from the 1520 logic of abolition, and by 1530 it had become a defense of a retained Mass, with examination and German hymns. The Reformed rival pressed on it from outside, though in the library that rival shows up only through the bodily presence in the Supper. Its service orders were never passed down into this library.

use_note.means: Promise and sign names the teaching that a sacrament is God's promise joined to an element and received by faith, with the seven sacraments cut to three and then two.
not_for: a sacrament as a work performed, or as a bare symbol
the presence doctrine at the Supper, which sits in witt.gravity.bodily-presence

uses.sentence: That confession was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document.
uses.paragraph: When a dispute needed settling, it did not move by vote the way you may imagine - and this is not a guess; we can show you exactly what the process looked like, once, because our own record holds one clear case entire. In 1530, before the Emperor himself at Augsburg, a confession of our teaching was read aloud and signed - not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of free cities together. That confession was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. Confession, written reply, written defense - argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, signed by those who held temporal authority alongside those who taught. That is the one case we can walk you through entirely, step by step, because our library holds every piece of it.
uses.record_text:
When belief was disputed in our own history, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this. In 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed -- not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense -- argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.
You say you have heard that a council basically voted Jesus into being God. Whatever happened at whichever council you mean, it did not happen among us, and it is not ours to speak to firsthand. The confession that Christ is truly God is not something our own history decided; it is something we received, already settled, centuries before our founder was born, and confessed as inherited teaching, not as a question we ourselves put to a vote.

use_note.means: This witness holds that our 1530 belief dispute was carried by a corporately signed confession, Rome's written reply, and our written Apology, not by a vote.
not_for: a narrated eyewitness account of the Diet's proceedings, the Emperor's reaction, or what was said in the room
the Roman Confutation's own words, which survive here only as quoted inside our Apology
a claim about what happened at the early ecumenical councils, which this world's records do not narrate
the confession's own signing story, which sits in witt.story.diet-of-augsburg-1530

And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

uses.sentence: He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power.
uses.paragraph: Every household under our catechism said the same words each week, in one voice: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other -- both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver; it cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him. And each of us says, in that same creed: He is my Lord! I am his very own. That claim is not private in the way you might think it -- it is said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue -- but it is not distant either; each believer says "my Lord," not only "our Lord."

uses.sentence: What would need careful qualification: the gap between prescription and practice.
uses.paragraph: What would need careful qualification: the gap between prescription and practice. We can document what households were told to do - morning prayer, weekly examination, the three parts said before food was given. A scholar would ask, rightly: did they actually do it? And we answer honestly: we do not know. The visitation reports that would answer that question exist in archives; they are not in our own library. So when we say 'every household says the three parts daily,' a rigorous reading would add: 'was instructed to' - and we have just made that distinction for you ourselves, because it is the truth.
uses.record_text:
Where is our own record thinnest? On what any actual household or parish did with what it was given. We can tell you exactly what a household was to do -- morning, table, and night. We can tell you exactly what a father was to ask his children and servants each week. That program is the most fully specified thing we hold, down to the hour. Whether it was kept is a different matter. The church in Saxony inspected its own parishes, starting in 1527, and wrote down what it found. Those reports exist. We do not hold them. What we hold instead is our founder's own testimony, given more than once, that common people held the Gospel too lightly, and that some pastors were negligent. That testimony is real. It is his own, said plainly and said more than once. But it is not, on its own, a report from any actual parish. We do not let it stand as one.
Two other places are just as thin. Our fellowship broke plainly with the cities who read the Supper differently. We can state our own position: Christ is truly present, in and under the bread and wine. But the argument itself, and what it felt like from our own side, has not come down to us. The cities' own names barely appear in what we hold at all. And no woman among us left her own word. There is one question, about coldness in prayer, asked at our founder's own table -- but even that was remembered by someone else, not written by her.
That is where we are thinnest. Not on what we were told to believe and do. On what was actually made of it, by real people, past our founder's own testimony about them.

use_note.means: The library holds the household catechism program in full but no visitation reports, no Marburg argument and no woman's own writing, so actual practice and reception are not told.
